question:
A heart transplant recipient requires long-term prophylaxis for cytomegalovirus
(CMV). He is prescribed oral valganciclovir. What is the primary pharmacokinetic advantage of valganciclovir over oral ganciclovir?

options.text: It has a much broader antiviral spectrum.
It does not cause bone marrow suppression.

It is a valyl ester prodrug that is well-absorbed orally and rapidly converted to
ganciclovir.
It is cleared by the liver, making it safe in renal failure.
It is a potent inhibitor of the CYP3A4 enzyme.

correctAnswer:
It is a valyl ester prodrug that is well-absorbed orally and rapidly converted to
ganciclovir.
englishExplanation:
Pharmacokinetics and Bioavailability:
Valganciclovir is the L-valyl ester prodrug of ganciclovir. Its primary advantage is
superior oral bioavailability (~60%) compared to oral ganciclovir (6-9%). It utilizes
intestinal peptide transporters (PEPT1 and PEPT2) for active absorption, whereas
ganciclovir relies on passive diffusion. Once absorbed, it is rapidly hydrolysed by cytoplasmic esterases in the intestine and liver to release active ganciclovir.
Elimination and Renal Safety:
Contrary to Option D, ganciclovir (the active metabolite) is eliminated primarily unchanged via glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion. Consequently, valganciclovir requires significant dose adjustment in renal impairment to prevent
toxicity.
Mechanism of Action:
Ganciclovir is a synthetic analogue of 2'-deoxyguanosine. Crucially, its initial phosphorylation is catalysed by the viral protein kinase pUL97 (conferring selectivity for
infected cells), followed by cellular kinases to form ganciclovir triphosphate. This
active metabolite competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerases and incorporates
into viral DNA, causing chain termination.
Clinical Pearl
Mechanism of Action:
The active drug, ganciclovir, is a guanosine analogue. It requires initial phosphorylation by the viral kinase pUL97 to become active, which subsequently inhibits viral
DNA polymerase.
Shared Toxicity Profile:
Valganciclovir carries the same toxicity profile as IV ganciclovir, most notably severe myelosuppression (neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia). Regular full
blood count monitoring is mandatory.
Clinical Indications:
It is the standard for oral CMV prophylaxis in transplant recipients and for stepdown therapy in CMV retinitis after initial IV treatment.
Resistant CMV Treatment:
Ganciclovir resistance (often via UL97 kinase mutations) requires treatment with
second-line agents such as Foscarnet or Cidofovir, which do not require viral
phosphorylation.

Renal Dose Adjustment:
Ganciclovir is renally excreted. Dosing of valganciclovir must be adjusted based on
creatinine clearance to avoid accumulation and increased marrow toxicity.
Teratogenicity:
Valganciclovir is teratogenic and carcinogenic. Effective contraception is required
during treatment and for at least 90 days post-cessation for men and 30 days for
women.
Bioavailability Equivalence:
The AUC (Area Under the Curve) of oral valganciclovir 900mg is comparable to that
of IV ganciclovir 5mg/kg, allowing for effective oral step-down therapy.
Selectivity vs Acyclovir:
Ganciclovir is effective against CMV because it is a substrate for the CMV-specific
kinase pUL97. Acyclovir is ineffective against CMV because the virus lacks the specific thymidine kinase required to activate acyclovir.
Letermovir Alternative:
Letermovir is a newer CMV terminase complex inhibitor used for prophylaxis, particularly in haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients. Unlike valganciclovir, it
does not cause myelosuppression.
Pre-emptive vs Prophylactic Therapy:
Prophylaxis involves administering antivirals to all high-risk patients (e.g., D+/R-).
Pre-emptive therapy involves monitoring viral load (PCR) and treating only when
viraemia reaches a specific threshold, reducing unnecessary drug exposure and
toxicity.
CMV Syndrome vs Disease:
CMV syndrome is defined by viraemia accompanied by constitutional symptoms
(fever, malaise, leukopenia) without end-organ damage. CMV disease implies tissue
invasion (e.g., pneumonitis, colitis, retinitis, hepatitis).

question: A 50-year-old on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed erythromycin. How might this affect her methotrexate levels?

options.text: Erythromycin will increase methotrexate levels.
Erythromycin will decrease methotrexate levels.
Erythromycin will have no effect on methotrexate levels.
Erythromycin will accelerate the renal clearance of methotrexate.

Erythromycin will convert methotrexate into an inactive metabolite.

Correct answerErythromycin will increase methotrexate levels.

correctAnswer: Erythromycin will increase methotrexate levels.
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Interaction:
Methotrexate is primarily excreted unchanged by the kidneys via glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion. Erythromycin inhibits organic anion transporters
(OAT1/OAT3) and P-glycoprotein (P-gp) in the renal tubules. This inhibition reduces the renal clearance of methotrexate, leading to accumulation and increased
toxicity. While erythromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor, methotrexate undergoes
negligible hepatic metabolism, making the CYP mechanism irrelevant in this specific interaction.
Clinical Consequences of Toxicity:
The accumulation of methotrexate primarily affects rapidly dividing cells. In the
ICU, this presents as severe bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia, neutropenic
sepsis), mucositis (stomatitis, GI ulceration, diarrhoea), and potentially acute hepatotoxicity or pneumonitis. Because methotrexate is excreted 80-90% unchanged by
the kidneys, any concurrent acute kidney injury creates a vicious cycle of accumulation and worsening toxicity.
Clinical Pearl
Macrolides Can Increase Methotrexate Levels:
Macrolides inhibit renal organic anion transporters (OATs) and P-glycoprotein, reducing methotrexate clearance. This interaction can precipitate severe toxicity even
in patients on stable long-term doses.
Methotrexate Toxicity is Serious:
High levels can cause life-threatening bone marrow suppression, mucositis, and
multi-organ failure.
Other Drugs that Increase MTX:
Other drugs that can increase methotrexate levels by reducing its renal clearance include NSAIDs, penicillins, and proton pump inhibitors.
Mechanism of Action:
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing the conversion
of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. This depletes the intracellular pool of reduced
folates required for purine and thymidylate synthesis, halting DNA replication.
Rescue Therapy Mechanism:
Folinic acid (leucovorin) is the specific antidote for methotrexate toxicity. It is a reduced folate that bypasses the DHFR block, allowing DNA synthesis to resume.
Folic acid is ineffective for acute rescue as it requires DHFR for activation.

Trimethoprim Contraindication:
Trimethoprim is an absolute contraindication in patients taking methotrexate. Both
drugs inhibit DHFR; co-prescription causes synergistic folate antagonism leading to
severe, rapid-onset bone marrow suppression and pancytopenia.
Third-Spacing Pharmacokinetics:
Methotrexate accumulates in 'third spaces' such as pleural effusions and ascites.
These reservoirs slowly release the drug back into the circulation, prolonging the
terminal half-life and increasing systemic toxicity risk.
NSAID Interaction Mechanism:
NSAIDs increase methotrexate toxicity via two mechanisms: inhibition of renal
prostaglandin synthesis (reducing afferent arteriolar flow and GFR) and direct competition for secretion by organic anion transporters in the proximal tubule.
Methotrexate Pneumonitis:
This is a hypersensitivity reaction that can occur at any dose and is not strictly dosedependent. It presents with dyspnoea, dry cough, and fever. It is distinct from the
dose-dependent bone marrow suppression.
Glucarpidase Role:
In cases of severe methotrexate toxicity with renal failure (delayed elimination),
glucarpidase can be used. It is a recombinant enzyme that hydrolyses extracellular
methotrexate into inactive metabolites (DAMPA and glutamate), providing an alternative clearance pathway.
Urine Alkalinisation:
Methotrexate and its metabolites can precipitate in renal tubules in acidic urine.
Maintaining high urine flow and alkalinisation (pH > 7.0) increases solubility and
prevents crystalluria-induced AKI.

question:
A patient with a severe metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.58, HCO₃ ⁻ 42 mEq/L) following
aggressive diuretic therapy is given intravenous acetazolamide. What is the primary mechanism of action of this drug?

options.text: It is a loop diuretic that blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter.
It is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks the ENaC channel.

It inhibits the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, primarily in the proximal convoluted
tubule.
It is an osmotic diuretic that pulls free water into the tubule.
It is an aldosterone antagonist.

correctAnswer:
It inhibits the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, primarily in the proximal convoluted
tubule.
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Acetazolamide is a potent reversible inhibitor of carbonic anhydrase, primarily affecting the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT). Under normal physiology, carbonic
anhydrase catalyses the dehydration of carbonic acid in the tubular lumen and the
hydration of carbon dioxide within the tubular cell, facilitating the reabsorption of
approximately 85% of filtered bicarbonate. By inhibiting this enzyme, acetazolamide blocks hydrogen ion secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption, resulting in alkaline urine (bicarbonaturia) and a hyperchloraemic normal anion gap metabolic
acidosis.
Clinical Utility in ICU:
In Critical Care, acetazolamide is primarily utilised to reverse contraction alkalosis
or post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis. By inducing metabolic acidosis, it theoretically increases respiratory drive (minute ventilation) in patients with COPD or those
being weaned from mechanical ventilation. However, the DIABOLO trial (Faisy et
al, JAMA 2016) — a randomised double-blind multicentre trial of 382 mechanically
ventilated COPD patients with metabolic alkalosis — found no statistically significant difference in duration of mechanical ventilation between acetazolamide and
placebo, despite acetazolamide significantly reducing serum bicarbonate and days
with metabolic alkalosis. The clinical benefit on weaning outcomes therefore remains unproven.
Clinical Pearl
Bicarbonate Wasting Effect:
Unlike loop and thiazide diuretics which induce metabolic alkalosis (contraction alkalosis), acetazolamide causes a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. While potassium-sparing diuretics can also promote acidosis, acetazolamide is unique in doing
so via direct proximal tubular bicarbonate wasting.
Weaning Adjunct:
Acetazolamide is used in the ICU to treat metabolic alkalosis in post-hypercapnic
COPD patients, as the alkalosis can suppress respiratory drive and impair weaning.
However, the DIABOLO trial showed no statistically significant reduction in mechanical ventilation duration, so its routine use for this indication remains
controversial.
Acute Mountain Sickness:

Acetazolamide is used for the prevention and treatment of acute mountain sickness.
By causing a metabolic acidosis, it stimulates the respiratory drive to compensate
for the hypoxia.
Intraocular Pressure:
Acetazolamide is used to treat glaucoma as it reduces the production of aqueous humour, thereby lowering intraocular pressure.
Hypokalaemia Risk:
By increasing sodium delivery to the distal tubule, acetazolamide can cause significant potassium wasting and hypokalaemia.
Self-Limiting Action:
The diuretic action of acetazolamide is self-limiting. Its efficacy depends on the filtered load of bicarbonate; as metabolic acidosis develops and plasma bicarbonate
levels fall, the drug loses its diuretic potency, typically within 2-3 days.
Hepatic Contraindication:
Acetazolamide is contraindicated in severe liver disease. By alkalinising the urine, it
reduces the trapping of ammonium in the renal tubule, decreasing ammonia excretion. This can raise systemic ammonia levels and precipitate hepatic
encephalopathy.
Salicylate Toxicity Trap:
Although acetazolamide alkalinises urine (which promotes salicylate excretion), it
causes systemic metabolic acidosis. This increases the non-ionised fraction of salicylate, facilitating its entry into the CNS and worsening toxicity. Therefore, it is generally avoided in salicylate poisoning.
Sulphonamide Cross-Reactivity:
Acetazolamide is a non-bacteriostatic sulphonamide derivative. While cross-reactivity in patients with antibiotic sulphonamide allergies is rare, caution is advised in
those with a history of anaphylaxis to sulphonamides.
Evidence Base:
The DIABOLO trial (Faisy et al, JAMA 2016) was a randomised double-blind multicentre trial of 382 COPD patients receiving mechanical ventilation with metabolic
alkalosis, comparing acetazolamide 500–1000 mg twice daily against placebo. The
primary outcome showed no statistically significant difference in duration of mechanical ventilation between groups, though acetazolamide significantly reduced
serum bicarbonate levels and the number of days with metabolic alkalosis. The
magnitude of difference was 16 hours in favour of acetazolamide — not statistically
significant — and the authors noted the study may have been underpowered to establish significance.

question:
A patient develops severe intra-abdominal hypertension (IAP 25 mmHg). In addition to the renal and cardiovascular effects, what is the direct effect of this high
IAP on respiratory mechanics?

options.text: It causes a significant increase in respiratory system compliance.
It causes a decrease in peak airway pressure but an increase in plateau pressure.

It elevates the diaphragm, reducing thoracic volume and decreasing chest wall
compliance.
It has no significant effect on respiratory mechanics.
It primarily causes an increase in physiological dead space.

correctAnswer:
It elevates the diaphragm, reducing thoracic volume and decreasing chest wall
compliance.
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
Increased intra-abdominal pressure is directly transmitted into the thoracic cavity,
pushing the hemidiaphragms upward. This compresses the lung bases (reducing
FRC) and dramatically decreases the compliance of the chest wall. To deliver a set
tidal volume into this stiff, non-compliant system, the ventilator must generate
much higher airway pressures (both peak and plateau), which can be mistaken for a
primary lung problem like ARDS.
Respiratory Mechanics:
Respiratory system compliance (C_rs) is the sum of lung compliance (C_L) and
chest wall compliance (C_cw), related by the series formula: 1/C_rs = 1/C_L +
1/C_cw. Intra-abdominal hypertension acts primarily by restricting the expansion
of the thoracic cavity via the diaphragm, thereby reducing C_cw. While secondary
atelectasis may eventually reduce C_L due to basal compression, the primary and
direct mechanical insult is the reduction in chest wall compliance. This distinction
is crucial because the lung parenchyma itself may remain relatively compliant despite high airway pressures.
Transpulmonary Pressure Significance:
In this setting, the high plateau pressure (P_plat) reflects the stiff chest wall rather
than stiff lungs. The transpulmonary pressure (P_tp = P_aw - P_pl) represents the
actual distending stress on the alveoli. Because pleural pressure (P_pl) is elevated
due to the high intra-abdominal pressure, the P_tp may be normal or even low despite a high P_plat. This protects the lung from barotrauma, meaning higher P_plat
limits may be tolerated than in primary ARDS.
Clinical Pearl
Compliance Interaction:
High intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) is a major cause of reduced respiratory system
compliance due to chest wall stiffening rather than primary lung pathology.
Clinical Suspicion:
In any ICU patient with unexpectedly high and rising airway pressures, intra-abdominal hypertension must be considered and measured, particularly if the abdomen is tense or distended.
Esophageal Manometry Role:

An esophageal balloon catheter can differentiate the cause of low compliance. In
Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS), manometry reveals very low chest wall
compliance with relatively preserved lung compliance.
Plateau Pressure Interpretation:
In patients with a stiff chest wall (from ACS or obesity), the plateau pressure may be
high (>30 cmH2O) even when the transpulmonary pressure (the actual distending
pressure of the lung) is within safe limits.
Decompressive Laparotomy Effects:
Decompressive laparotomy for ACS typically results in an immediate and dramatic
improvement in respiratory mechanics, characterised by a significant drop in peak
and plateau airway pressures.
IAH and ACS Definitions:
Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is defined as a sustained IAP >= 12 mmHg.
Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS) is defined as a sustained IAP > 20
mmHg associated with new organ dysfunction.
IAP Measurement Technique:
Current WSACS guidelines mandate zeroing the pressure transducer at the iliac
crest in the mid-axillary line, rather than the symphysis pubis.
Polycompartment Physiology:
High IAP impairs venous return from the head due to elevated intrathoracic pressure. This can raise intracranial pressure (ICP) and reduce cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), linking abdominal and cerebral compartments.
Abdominal Perfusion Pressure:
Abdominal Perfusion Pressure (APP) is calculated as MAP minus IAP. A target APP
>= 60 mmHg is suggested to maintain adequate visceral perfusion, which may require higher MAP targets in patients with IAH.
Renal Filtration Gradient:
Oliguria in IAH is caused by both reduced cardiac output and direct renal compression. The Filtration Gradient (FG = MAP - IAP) determines glomerular filtration; as
IAP rises, higher MAP is required to maintain urine output.
Medical Management Hierarchy:
Before surgical decompression, medical management includes: improving abdominal wall compliance (sedation, analgesia, neuromuscular blockade), evacuating intraluminal contents (NG tube, rectal tube, enemas), and evacuating extraluminal
collections (percutaneous drainage).
Fluid Stewardship:

While initial resuscitation requires fluids, secondary IAH is often driven by fluid
overload and bowel oedema. A strategy of fluid restriction and dereproximation (diuretics or renal replacement therapy) is key in the management phase.

question:
The Fowler method is a physiological technique used to measure which specific
component of the respiratory dead space?

options.text: The physiological dead space
The alveolar dead space
The anatomical dead space
The shunt fraction

The apparatus dead space of the ventilator

Correct answerThe anatomical dead space

correctAnswer: The anatomical dead space
englishExplanation:
The Fowler Method (Single-Breath Nitrogen Washout):
The Fowler method (single-breath nitrogen washout) measures anatomical dead
space. The subject inspires a single breath of 100% oxygen (0% nitrogen) and then
exhales into a nitrogen analyzer. The concentration of nitrogen in the exhaled air is
plotted against volume. An equal-area technique is used to determine the midpoint
of the transition (Phase II) between pure dead space gas (0% nitrogen) and alveolar
gas. The volume exhaled up to this vertical line represents the anatomical dead
space.
Comparison with Bohr Equation:
While Fowler measures anatomical dead space (conducting airways), the Bohr
equation measures physiological dead space (anatomical + alveolar). The Bohr
equation relies on the principle that CO₂ is exhaled only from perfused alveoli, using the ratio of arterial to mixed expired CO₂.
Phases of the Nitrogen Washout Curve:
The expiratory curve has four phases:
1. Phase I: Pure dead space gas (0% N₂).
2. Phase II: Rapid rise in N₂ (mixture of dead space and alveolar gas).
3. Phase III: Alveolar plateau (slow rise).
4. Phase IV: Closing volume (abrupt rise in N₂ due to closure of basal airways).
Clinical Pearl
Fowler Method Specificity:
The Fowler method specifically measures the volume of the conducting airways (trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles) representing the anatomical dead space.
Anatomical vs. Alveolar Dead Space:
Physiological Dead Space = Anatomical Dead Space + Alveolar Dead Space. The
Fowler method measures the anatomical component, while the Bohr equation measures the total physiological dead space. Alveolar dead space is calculated as the difference between the two.
Normal Anatomical Dead Space:
Anatomical dead space is approximately 2.2 mL/kg of ideal body weight (roughly
150 mL in a 70 kg adult). It constitutes about 30% of the tidal volume in a healthy
subject.
Closing Volume Significance:

The single-breath nitrogen washout test also identifies the 'Closing Volume' (Phase
IV). This represents the lung volume at which small airways in the dependent lung
zones begin to close. An increased closing volume (encroaching on tidal breathing)
is a key mechanism of hypoxemia in age, smoking, and obesity.
Factors Increasing Anatomical Dead Space:
Anatomical dead space increases with lung volume (radial traction on airways),
neck extension, bronchodilators (increased airway caliber), and upright posture.
Apparatus Dead Space:
Apparatus dead space (HME filters, catheter mounts, elbow connectors) extends the
anatomical dead space. In paediatrics or ARDS with low tidal volumes, this mechanical dead space significantly impacts CO₂ clearance.
Phase III Slope Significance:
The slope of the alveolar plateau (Phase III) indicates the uniformity of gas distribution. A steep slope suggests uneven emptying of alveoli with different time constants, which is characteristic of obstructive lung diseases like COPD or asthma.
Bohr vs Enghoff Modification:
The original Bohr equation requires mean alveolar CO2 (PACO2), which is difficult
to measure directly. The Enghoff modification substitutes arterial CO2 (PaCO2) for
PACO2. This makes the calculation practical but means the result includes both
anatomical and alveolar dead space (physiological dead space).
Dead Space in Health vs Disease:
In healthy individuals, anatomical and physiological dead space are nearly identical
because alveolar dead space is negligible. In respiratory disease (e.g., pulmonary
embolism, ARDS), alveolar dead space increases significantly, causing physiological
dead space to exceed anatomical dead space.
West Zones and Dead Space:
Alveolar dead space is most prominent in West Zone 1 (apices), where alveolar pressure exceeds pulmonary arterial pressure, causing ventilation without perfusion.
This effect is exacerbated by hypovolaemia or high PEEP.
Cardiogenic Oscillations:
Small fluctuations often seen in Phase III of the nitrogen washout curve are termed
cardiogenic oscillations. These are caused by the mechanical action of the heart
beating against the lungs, which aids in gas mixing.

question: Which statement about the diagnostic workup for a suspected aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is NOT true?

options.text: A non-contrast head CT is the first-line investigation for a patient with a 'thunderclap' headache.

If the initial CT is negative but performed > 6 hours from symptom onset, a
lumbar puncture (LP) is required to rule out SAH.

The characteristic finding on LP that indicates SAH is xanthochromia (yellow
discolouration of the CSF).

If the initial CT scan, performed within 6 hours of a thunderclap headache, is
negative, SAH is definitively ruled out and no further tests are needed.
An LP for SAH should be performed at least 12 hours after symptom onset to allow time for xanthochromia to develop.

correctAnswer:
If the initial CT scan, performed within 6 hours of a thunderclap headache, is
negative, SAH is definitively ruled out and no further tests are needed.
englishExplanation:
The 6-Hour CT Rule (NICE NG228):
NICE NG228 states that clinicians should not routinely offer a lumbar puncture to
patients with a negative head CT performed within 6 hours of symptom onset. This
is based on evidence showing modern CT scanners have a sensitivity approaching
100% in this window. However, this does not 'definitively rule out' SAH in all circumstances. Clinical judgment remains essential; if the scan quality is poor, the patient has severe anaemia (causing acute blood to appear isodense), or clinical suspicion remains extremely high, an LP may still be indicated. The guideline advises
against 'routine' LP, but acknowledges specific high-risk exceptions.
Physiology of Xanthochromia:
The 12-hour wait for lumbar puncture is dictated by the physiology of haemoglobin
breakdown. Red blood cells lyse to release oxyhaemoglobin (pink), which is then
converted by the enzyme haem oxygenase into bilirubin (yellow/xanthochromic).
This enzymatic process occurs in vivo within the CSF and takes approximately 12
hours to reach detectable levels. Performing an LP earlier may result in a false negative for xanthochromia.
CT Sensitivity Decline:
CT sensitivity for SAH is highest (>98%) in the first 6 hours. It declines progressively to approximately 50% by 1 week. This reduction occurs because blood mixes
with CSF, circulates away from the subarachnoid space, and undergoes degradation,
reducing its density contrast against brain tissue. Therefore, a negative CT in a patient presenting >6 hours after headache onset requires an LP to exclude SAH.
Clinical Pearl
The 6-Hour CT Rule:
A negative, high-quality CT performed within 6 hours of a thunderclap headache
makes SAH extremely unlikely, and an LP may be omitted if clinical suspicion is
low.
Delayed Presentation Management:
The sensitivity of CT decreases significantly over time (to ~50% by 1 week) due to
CSF circulation and blood degradation. Therefore, if the CT is performed >6 hours
after symptom onset and is negative, an LP is mandatory to exclude SAH.
Xanthochromia vs Traumatic Tap:

The presence of red blood cells in the CSF can result from a traumatic tap.
Xanthochromia, the yellow staining from RBC breakdown (bilirubin), is the definitive sign of a true SAH as it indicates blood has been present in the CSF long enough
to be metabolised.
Timing of Lumbar Puncture:
An LP should be performed at least 12 hours after symptom onset. This allows sufficient time for the enzymatic conversion of oxyhaemoglobin to bilirubin (xanthochromia) by haem oxygenase.
Vascular Imaging Indication:
Once SAH is diagnosed (by CT or LP), the immediate next step is CT angiography
(CTA) to identify the underlying aneurysm or vascular malformation and guide
intervention.
Spectrophotometry Standard:
UK guidelines mandate the use of spectrophotometry to detect xanthochromia
(bilirubin). Visual inspection of CSF supernatant is unreliable and has a lower sensitivity for detecting subtle bilirubin presence.
Impact of Severe Anaemia:
In patients with severe anaemia (Hb <100 g/L, and especially <70 g/L), acute blood
may appear isodense to brain tissue on CT rather than hyperdense. This can lead to
a false-negative CT scan even within the 6-hour window.
False Positive Xanthochromia:
Xanthochromia can be falsely positive in the presence of systemic jaundice (serum
bilirubin >100-150 micromol/L crossing the blood-brain barrier) or very high CSF
protein levels (>1.5 g/L).
Perimesencephalic SAH:
This is a distinct subset of non-aneurysmal SAH where blood is confined to the midbrain cisterns. It typically has a benign clinical course, normal angiography, and a
very low risk of re-bleeding compared to aneurysmal SAH.
Sentinel Headache:
A 'sentinel headache' (a sudden, severe headache preceding the major rupture by
days or weeks) occurs in 10-40% of patients. It represents a minor leak or aneurysm
wall expansion and is a critical missed opportunity for early diagnosis.

question:
A patient with a 40% total body surface area burn from 3 weeks ago requires intubation. Which statement about the use of suxamethonium (succinylcholine) in
this patient is true?

options.text:
Suxamethonium is safe to use as the risk of hyperkalemia resolves within 72
hours of a burn injury.
The expected rise in serum potassium in a normal patient is 2-3 mmol/L.

The hyperkalemic response is due to suxamethonium's action on muscarinic
receptors.

The risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia is due to the systemic upregulation of
extrajunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in skeletal muscle.
Administering a 'defasciculating' dose of a non-depolarizing agent will completely prevent the hyperkalemic response.

correctAnswer:
The risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia is due to the systemic upregulation of
extrajunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in skeletal muscle.
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
In major burns (>10% TBSA), denervation-like changes occur systemically. Skeletal
muscle cells revert to a fetal phenotype, expressing immature nicotinic acetylcholine
receptors (nAChRs) throughout the sarcolemma (extrajunctional), not just at the
neuromuscular junction. These immature receptors (containing a gamma subunit
instead of an epsilon subunit) have a prolonged open time and are easily depolarized by suxamethonium, leading to massive, uncontrolled potassium efflux.
Timeline of Risk:
Suxamethonium is generally considered safe within the first 24 hours following a
burn injury. The upregulation of extrajunctional receptors becomes clinically significant after 24-48 hours, peaks between 10 and 50 days, and can persist for months
to years (until the burn is fully healed and metabolic stress subsides).
Magnitude of Potassium Rise:
In healthy individuals, suxamethonium causes a transient serum potassium increase of approximately 0.5 mmol/L. In patients with upregulated extrajunctional
receptors (burns, denervation, crush injury), the rise can be catastrophic (often >35 mmol/L), leading to cardiac arrest.
Clinical Pearl
Absolute Contraindications:
Suxamethonium is absolutely contraindicated in major burns, crush injuries, spinal
cord injuries, and strokes after the first 24-48 hours. It is also contraindicated in
myopathies (e.g., Duchenne) or a history of malignant hyperthermia.
Mechanism of Hyperkalemia:
The mechanism is the proliferation of 'fetal' extrajunctional nicotinic receptors
(containing a gamma subunit) which have longer channel open times than mature
(epsilon subunit) receptors, leading to exaggerated potassium efflux.
Duration of Risk:
The period of risk for severe hyperkalemia can last for many months to years after
the initial injury, persisting until the burn is fully healed and metabolic stress has
resolved.
Physiological Potassium Flux:
In a healthy individual, suxamethonium causes a transient serum potassium increase of approximately 0.5 mmol/L, which is clinically insignificant.

Defasciculation Limitations:
Administering a 'defasciculating' dose of a non-depolarizing agent does NOT prevent hyperkalemia in susceptible patients. The potassium efflux occurs via extrajunctional receptors independent of visible fasciculations.
Systemic Receptor Distribution:
Receptor upregulation in burns is a systemic phenomenon mediated by circulating
factors. It affects all skeletal muscle, not just the muscle underlying the burned skin.
Rocuronium Alternative:
In patients with contraindications to suxamethonium, rocuronium at a dose of 1.2
mg/kg provides intubating conditions within 60 seconds (modified rapid sequence
induction).
ICU-Acquired Weakness:
Patients with critical illness polyneuropathy/myopathy or prolonged immobilization (>2 weeks) in the ICU also develop extrajunctional receptor upregulation and
are at risk of suxamethonium-induced hyperkalemia.
Plasma Cholinesterase Deficiency:
This is a separate contraindication involving prolonged paralysis (suxamethonium
apnoea) rather than hyperkalemia. It may be congenital (genetic variants) or acquired (e.g., severe liver failure, pregnancy).
Treatment of Suxamethonium Hyperkalemia:
Management involves standard hyperkalemia protocols: IV calcium (chloride or
gluconate) to stabilise the myocardium, followed by insulin/dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly.

question:
A 7-month-old infant presents with infantile spasms (West syndrome). A thorough skin examination reveals several hypopigmented 'ash-leaf' spots. An MRI
shows cortical tubers and subependymal nodules. This child is at a high risk of
developing which of the following life-threatening complications later in life?

options.text: Aortic dissection
Malignant spinal cord compression
Spontaneous renal haemorrhage from an angiomyolipoma
Aplastic anaemia

Fulminant hepatic failure

Correct answerSpontaneous renal haemorrhage from an angiomyolipoma

correctAnswer: Spontaneous renal haemorrhage from an angiomyolipoma
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology and Renal Complications:
Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by
mutations in TSC1 or TSC2, leading to uninhibited mTOR pathway activation and
hamartoma growth. Renal angiomyolipomas (AMLs) occur in up to 80% of adults.
These lesions contain abnormal vasculature prone to aneurysm formation due to
elastin-poor vessel walls. Spontaneous rupture results in life-threatening retroperitoneal haemorrhage (Wunderlich syndrome). Risk factors for haemorrhage include
tumour size >4 cm and aneurysm size >5 mm. Embolization or mTOR inhibitors are
preferred over nephrectomy to preserve renal function.
Other Systemic Complications:
While cardiac rhabdomyomas are common in infancy, they typically regress spontaneously. Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a major risk for adult females, causing cystic lung destruction and pneumothorax. Subependymal Giant Cell
Astrocytomas (SEGAs) can cause obstructive hydrocephalus.
Analysis of Other Options:
Aortic dissection is associated with connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not TSC. Malignant spinal cord compression is a
complication of metastatic cancer. Aplastic anaemia is associated with Fanconi
anaemia or drug toxicity. Fulminant hepatic failure is not a feature of TSC, though
hepatic AMLs can occur rarely.
Clinical Pearl
Renal Angiomyolipoma (AML) Management:
Renal AMLs occur in 80% of TSC patients. Active surveillance is required; intervention (mTOR inhibitors or embolization) is indicated for AMLs >3-4 cm to prevent
Wunderlich syndrome (massive retroperitoneal haemorrhage). Nephron-sparing
approaches are critical as CKD is a leading cause of mortality.
Pulmonary Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM):
LAM affects predominantly females with TSC (up to 30-40%). It is characterised by
cystic lung destruction, presenting with dyspnoea or recurrent pneumothorax. Adult
females with TSC require screening with High-Resolution CT (HRCT) chest.
Neurological Features & SEGA:
Epilepsy affects 90% of patients (often infantile spasms/West syndrome).
Subependymal Giant Cell Astrocytomas (SEGAs) occur in 10-15%, typically near the

Foramen of Monro. Serial MRI surveillance is mandatory to detect growth and prevent acute hydrocephalus.
Cardiac Rhabdomyomas:
These are the most common primary cardiac tumour in foetuses and neonates with
TSC. Unlike other TSC hamartomas, the vast majority regress spontaneously during
childhood. Intervention is only required for severe outflow obstruction or intractable arrhythmias.
Mechanism and Targeted Therapy:
TSC is caused by loss of inhibition of the mTOR pathway (TSC1/TSC2 mutations).
This pathophysiology allows for targeted therapy with mTOR inhibitors (e.g.,
everolimus), which are now licensed in the UK for treating SEGAs and renal AMLs
not amenable to surgery.
Cutaneous Markers:
Classic skin signs include ash-leaf spots (hypopigmented macules enhanced by
Wood's lamp), facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), Shagreen patches (connective tissue naevus), and periungual fibromas (Koenen's tumours).
Genetics and Inheritance:
TSC is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity. However, approximately
two-thirds of cases arise from de novo mutations. TSC2 mutations generally present
with a more severe phenotype than TSC1.
TSC-Associated Neuropsychiatric Disorders (TAND):
A significant proportion of patients suffer from autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, and behavioural problems. These require multidisciplinary management alongside physical complications.
Wunderlich Syndrome:
Defined as spontaneous non-traumatic renal haemorrhage into the subcapsular and
perirenal spaces. While renal cell carcinoma and vasculitis are causes, renal AML is
the most common aetiology in benign pathology.
Differentiation of Renal Masses:
Renal AMLs are distinguished from renal cell carcinoma on CT/MRI by the presence of macroscopic fat (negative Hounsfield units). Fat-poor AMLs can be difficult
to distinguish and may require biopsy.

question:
An 80-year-old man who suffered an acute anterior wall myocardial infarction
five days ago suddenly develops severe hypotension, pulmonary edema, and a
new, loud, harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border. Which statement
regarding this likely complication is INCORRECT?

options.text: The timing of the event, 3-7 days post-MI, is classic for a mechanical complication like VSR.
This is an apical or anterior septal rupture, which is typically caused by an occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery.

The definitive treatment is urgent surgical repair, as medical management alone
has a very high mortality rate.
An inferior wall MI is the most common cause of anterior septal ruptures.

Echocardiography will show a left-to-right shunt across the interventricular
septum.

Correct answerAn inferior wall MI is the most common cause of anterior septal ruptures.

correctAnswer: An inferior wall MI is the most common cause of anterior septal ruptures.
englishExplanation:
Anatomy and Pathophysiology:
Ventricular Septal Rupture (VSR) location correlates with the infarcting artery.
Anterior VSRs (apical) result from Left Anterior Descending (LAD) occlusion.
Inferior/Basal VSRs result from Right Coronary Artery (RCA) or dominant Left
Circumflex (LCx) occlusion. Therefore, statement D is incorrect because inferior
MIs do not cause anterior ruptures.
Haemodynamic Mechanism:
The left-to-right shunt through the ruptured septum causes acute volume overload
of the right ventricle and pulmonary circulation, leading to biventricular failure. The
magnitude of the shunt (Qp:Qs ratio) determines the degree of haemodynamic compromise. Afterload reduction (e.g. with an IABP) decreases the shunt fraction and
improves forward systemic output.
Clinical Presentation and Timing:
VSR typically presents 3-5 days post-MI (range 1-14 days) with sudden haemodynamic collapse (biventricular failure) and a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left
sternal border. It is a mechanical complication distinct from papillary muscle rupture (PMR) and free wall rupture.
Management Principles:
Medical management alone carries >90% mortality. Stabilisation focuses on afterload reduction to decrease the left-to-right shunt fraction (Qp:Qs) and improve systemic flow. An Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (IABP) is the first-line mechanical support, providing afterload reduction (systolic unloading) and augmenting coronary
perfusion (diastolic augmentation). Urgent surgical repair is the definitive
treatment.
Clinical Pearl
The '3 M's' of Post-MI Mechanical Complications:
The '3 M's' of mechanical complications causing a new murmur after MI are: (1)
Mitral regurgitation — from papillary muscle rupture, loudest at the apex radiating to the axilla; (2) Myocardial free wall rupture — typically presents with
PEA arrest and tamponade rather than a murmur, but included as a mechanical
complication; (3) Mural (septal) rupture — i.e. Ventricular Septal Rupture
(VSR), with a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border. "Mural" here
refers to the interventricular septum (the wall between the ventricles). All three typically occur 3–7 days post-MI.

Anterior vs. Posterior VSR:
Anterior ruptures (from LAD infarcts) are more common. Posterior ruptures (from
RCA infarcts) are less common but often have a worse prognosis due to more complex surgical repair.
Role of IABP:
An intra-aortic balloon pump is a crucial bridge to surgery. By reducing afterload, it
helps to decrease the amount of left-to-right shunting and improve forward systemic blood flow.
Surgery is Urgent:
Without emergent surgical repair, mortality from post-infarction VSR approaches
90%.
VSR vs. Papillary Muscle Rupture:
The VSR murmur is typically loudest at the left sternal border. The murmur of acute
mitral regurgitation is typically loudest at the apex and radiates to the axilla.
Echocardiography is definitive.
Palpable Thrill Specificity:
A palpable systolic thrill at the left sternal border is present in approximately 50%
of patients with VSR but is rare in acute mitral regurgitation. This physical sign can
help distinguish the two at the bedside before echocardiography.
Oximetry Run-Up (Step-Up):
Right heart catheterisation (PAC) in VSR will show an oxygen saturation 'step-up'
between the right atrium and right ventricle/pulmonary artery due to the left-toright shunt of oxygenated blood. A step-up of >5% is diagnostic.
VSR Risk Factors:
Risk factors for VSR include advanced age, female sex, single-vessel disease, and
first myocardial infarction. The absence of pre-existing collateral circulation in a
first MI makes the myocardium more susceptible to transmural necrosis and subsequent rupture.
Haemodynamic Profile:
In VSR, pulmonary artery catheterisation typically reveals elevated right-sided pressures (CVP and PAP) due to the shunt and RV failure, alongside a low cardiac index.
Unlike acute mitral regurgitation, which produces giant 'v' waves on the PCWP
trace, VSR is primarily characterised by the oxygen saturation step-up.

question:
Which of the following conditions or substances is NOT a recognized cause of
hypercalcemia?

options.text: Thiazide diuretics
Malignancy (e.g., through PTHrP production)
Lithium therapy
Ethylene glycol poisoning

Sarcoidosis (and other granulomatous diseases)

Correct answerEthylene glycol poisoning

correctAnswer: Ethylene glycol poisoning
englishExplanation:
Ethylene Glycol and Calcium:
Ethylene glycol poisoning is a classic cause of severe hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia. It is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycolic acid and subsequently
to oxalic acid. Oxalic acid chelates serum calcium to form insoluble calcium oxalate
crystals. This precipitation leads to profound hypocalcemia and crystal deposition in
renal tubules, causing acute kidney injury.
Mechanisms of Hypercalcemia in Other Options:
Thiazide diuretics increase renal calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule and can
unmask primary hyperparathyroidism. Lithium reduces the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in the parathyroid glands, raising the set-point for
PTH release. Malignancy causes hypercalcemia primarily via secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) or direct osteolytic metastasis. Granulomatous diseases (e.g.,
Sarcoidosis) cause hypercalcemia through the unregulated production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D by activated macrophages.
Mechanisms of Hypercalcemia in Other Options:
Thiazide diuretics increase renal calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule and can
unmask primary hyperparathyroidism. Lithium reduces the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in the parathyroid glands, raising the set-point for
PTH release. Malignancy causes hypercalcemia primarily via secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) or direct osteolytic metastasis. Granulomatous diseases (e.g.,
Sarcoidosis) cause hypercalcemia through the unregulated production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D by activated macrophages.
Clinical Pearl
Clinical Presentation Mnemonic:
The classic mnemonic for hypercalcemia symptoms is 'Stones, Bones, Groans,
Thrones, and Psychiatric Overtones': kidney stones, bone pain, abdominal
pain/constipation, polyuria, and confusion/depression.
Diagnostic Approach:
The first step in working up hypercalcemia is always to measure an intact PTH level.
A high or inappropriately normal PTH suggests primary hyperparathyroidism. A
low PTH points to a non-parathyroid cause (e.g., malignancy, vitamin D toxicity).
Granulomatous Mechanism:
In diseases like sarcoidosis, activated macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase,
leading to excess production of active Vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol)

and subsequent hypercalcemia.
Ethylene Glycol Presentation:
The combination of a severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis and hypocalcemia
should raise strong suspicion for ethylene glycol poisoning.
Immobilization Hypercalcemia:
Prolonged, strict immobilization can cause hypercalcemia due to increased bone resorption, particularly in adolescents or patients with high bone turnover (e.g.,
Paget's disease).
ECG Changes in Calcium Disorders:
Hypercalcemia typically causes shortening of the QT interval. Conversely, the
hypocalcemia seen in ethylene glycol poisoning causes QT prolongation.
Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (FHH):
Consider FHH in asymptomatic mild hypercalcemia with normal/high PTH. Unlike
primary hyperparathyroidism, FHH presents with low urinary calcium excretion
(Calcium/Creatinine clearance ratio < 0.01).
Calcium-Alkali Syndrome:
Previously known as Milk-Alkali syndrome, this presents with the triad of hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and renal insufficiency. It is increasingly common due to
the use of calcium carbonate for osteoporosis or dyspepsia.
Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism:
This occurs when parathyroid hyperplasia becomes autonomous after a prolonged
period of secondary hyperparathyroidism (e.g., in end-stage renal disease). It is
characterised by hypercalcemia with very high PTH levels.
Adrenal Insufficiency:
Hypercalcemia can occur in Addisonian crisis. The mechanism involves volume
contraction (increasing renal calcium reabsorption) and reduced glucocorticoid-mediated antagonism of vitamin D.
Thyrotoxicosis:
Mild hypercalcemia occurs in up to 20% of thyrotoxic patients due to thyroid hormone-mediated increase in bone turnover and resorption.
Calcitonin Tachyphylaxis:
While calcitonin rapidly lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts and increasing renal excretion, its effect is transient due to receptor downregulation (tachyphylaxis), typically limiting efficacy to 48 hours.
Denosumab Mechanism:
Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL (Receptor Activator of
Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Ligand). It inhibits osteoclast maturation and survival,

making it a potent option for refractory hypercalcemia of malignancy.

question:
A 47-year-old man presents with blurred vision and headache after drinking
'homemade alcohol.' Labs show a pH of 7.20, HCO₃ ⁻ of 15 mmol/L, and a calculated osmolar gap. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ethylene glycol poisoning
Methanol poisoning
Isopropanol poisoning
Diabetic ketoacidosis

Lactic acidosis

Correct answerMethanol poisoning

correctAnswer: Methanol poisoning
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
The combination of ingesting an unknown alcohol, developing a severe metabolic
acidosis with an osmolar gap, and the specific complaint of visual disturbances is
pathognomonic for methanol poisoning.
Pathophysiology Review:
Methanol is metabolised by ADH to formaldehyde and then to formic acid. The parent alcohol (methanol) is osmotically active and creates the osmolar gap. The metabolite (formic acid) is a strong acid that causes the high anion gap metabolic acidosis and is specifically toxic to the optic nerve.
Clinical Correlation:
The patient's severe headache and blurred vision are direct consequences of the
formic acid toxicity. The history of 'homemade alcohol' is classic, as moonshine or
improperly distilled spirits can be contaminated with methanol. The tachypnoea is a
compensatory response (Kussmaul breathing) to the severe metabolic acidosis.
Analysis of Options:
Ethylene glycol (A) is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acid, causing renal failure
(calcium oxalate deposition) rather than visual loss. Isopropanol (C) is metabolised
to acetone, causing a high osmolar gap and ketosis, but notably does NOT cause
metabolic acidosis. DKA (D) presents with hyperglycaemia and ketonuria; while it
causes a HAGMA, visual symptoms are not a primary feature of the toxicity.
Clinical Pearl
Visual Toxicity Presentation:
The combination of apparent alcohol intoxication and visual complaints (blurred vision, 'snowstorm' vision, or scotoma) should immediately raise suspicion for
methanol poisoning.
Calculate the Gaps:
In any patient with an unexplained metabolic acidosis, you must calculate both the
anion gap and the osmolar gap. The presence of both an elevated anion gap and an
elevated osmolar gap (a 'gap-gap') is highly suggestive of a toxic alcohol ingestion.
Latent Period:
There is often a latent period (6-24 hours) between the ingestion of methanol and
the onset of symptoms. This is the time it takes for the methanol to be metabolised
into formic acid.
Mechanism of Fomepizole:

Fomepizole acts as a potent competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH).
Early administration blocks the conversion of methanol to toxic formic acid, preventing metabolic acidosis and end-organ damage.
Cofactor Replacement:
Folinic acid (or folic acid) should be administered in methanol poisoning to enhance
the conversion of toxic formate to carbon dioxide and water.
Indications for Haemodialysis:
According to TOXBASE, haemodialysis is indicated for methanol poisoning if there
is visual impairment, severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.30), renal failure, or a blood
methanol concentration >500 mg/L.
Osmolar Gap Calculation:
The osmolar gap is the difference between measured and calculated osmolality.
Calculated osmolality = (2 x Na) + Urea + Glucose (all in mmol/L). A gap greater
than 10 mOsm/kg is considered abnormal and suggests the presence of an unmeasured osmotically active substance.
The 'Teeter-Totter' Effect:
In toxic alcohol ingestion, there is an inverse relationship between the osmolar gap
and the anion gap over time. Early after ingestion, the parent alcohol causes a high
osmolar gap but minimal acidosis. As metabolism proceeds, the parent alcohol decreases (lowering the osmolar gap) while toxic acid metabolites accumulate (raising
the anion gap).
Isopropanol Distinction:
Isopropanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetone. Acetone is a ketone but not an acid. Therefore, isopropanol poisoning presents with a high osmolar
gap and ketosis/ketonuria, but notably without metabolic acidosis.
Putaminal Necrosis:
Bilateral putaminal necrosis (haemorrhage or oedema in the basal ganglia) is a
characteristic late neuroimaging finding in severe methanol poisoning, resulting
from the direct histotoxic effects of formic acid.

question:
A 2-year-old is brought to the ED 8 hours after ingesting an unknown number of
iron tablets. After an initial period of vomiting, he now appears deceptively well,

with his GI symptoms resolved. His parents are requesting to take him home.
This clinical phase is highly concerning for which stage of iron toxicity?

options.text: Stage 1 (Gastrointestinal phase)
Stage 2 (Latent phase)
Stage 3 (Metabolic/Shock phase)
Stage 4 (Hepatic phase)

This signifies resolution of the toxicity.

Correct answerStage 2 (Latent phase)

correctAnswer: Stage 2 (Latent phase)
englishExplanation:
Clinical Context:
Iron toxicity classically follows five clinical stages, though these may overlap. The
scenario describes Stage 2 (Latent Phase), typically occurring 6–24 hours post-ingestion. Following initial GI irritation (Stage 1), symptoms may resolve, providing
false reassurance while intracellular toxicity (mitochondrial injury) progresses. This
phase often precedes overt shock and metabolic acidosis.
Stages of Iron Toxicity:
Stage 1 (0–6h): Gastrointestinal irritation (vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain).
Stage 2 (6–24h): Latent phase (apparent resolution of GI symptoms; subclinical hypoperfusion and metabolic acidosis may develop).
Stage 3 (6–72h): Shock and metabolic acidosis (cardiovascular collapse, coagulopathy, renal failure, high anion gap acidosis).
Stage 4 (12–96h): Hepatotoxicity (hepatic necrosis, jaundice, coagulopathy).
Stage 5 (2–8 weeks): Gastrointestinal scarring (pyloric stenosis or strictures).
Management Principles:
Management involves aggressive resuscitation, whole bowel irrigation for significant radiopaque burdens, and chelation with desferrioxamine. Chelation is indicated for severe toxicity (shock, reduced GCS), persistent metabolic acidosis, or
serum iron >90 µmol/L (approx. 5 mg/L).
Pathophysiology:
Free iron is directly corrosive to the GI mucosa, causing the initial symptoms. Once
absorbed, it exceeds the binding capacity of transferrin and circulates as free iron.
This free iron acts as a catalyst in the Fenton reaction, generating hydroxyl free radicals that cause oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and mitochondrial dysfunction.
The uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation leads to anaerobic metabolism and
lactate production, contributing to the profound metabolic acidosis seen in Stage 3.
Clinical Pearl
Deceptive Clinical Resolution:
The latent phase (Stage 2) is characterised by the resolution of GI symptoms, which
can provide false reassurance. However, intracellular toxicity is ongoing during this
period, often manifesting as subclinical hypoperfusion or metabolic acidosis before
overt shock develops.
Observation Requirements:

Symptomatic patients or those with significant ingestions require observation for at
least 12 hours. If asymptomatic at 6 hours post-ingestion with normal vital signs
and levels, discharge may be considered, but the presence of initial symptoms warrants extended monitoring for the latent phase.
Whole Bowel Irrigation:
If an abdominal X-ray shows a large number of tablets still in the gut, whole bowel
irrigation is a key intervention to prevent further absorption.
Chelation Indications:
Desferrioxamine is the chelator of choice. Indications include: shock, reduced level
of consciousness, metabolic acidosis, or serum iron >90 µmol/L (5 mg/L).
Serum Iron Monitoring:
Serum iron levels should be monitored, with the peak concentration typically occurring 4-6 hours post-ingestion, which is at the beginning of the latent phase.
Acidosis Pathophysiology:
Iron toxicity causes a high anion gap metabolic acidosis via two mechanisms: uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation (leading to anaerobic metabolism and lactate
production) and the hydration of free ferric ions releasing protons.
Long-term Complications:
Survivors of severe acute toxicity may present 2–8 weeks later with gastric outlet
obstruction or bowel obstruction due to stricture formation (Stage 5).
Toxicity Thresholds:
Ingestions <20 mg/kg elemental iron are typically asymptomatic. 20–60 mg/kg
causes mild to moderate GI symptoms. >60 mg/kg is potentially life-threatening.
Always calculate the elemental iron dose.
Elemental Iron Content:
To calculate the toxic dose, one must know the percentage of elemental iron in the
ingested salt: Ferrous Fumarate (~33%), Ferrous Sulfate (~20%), and Ferrous
Gluconate (~12%).
Fenton Reaction:
Free iron acts as a catalyst in the Fenton reaction, converting hydrogen peroxide
into highly reactive hydroxyl radicals. This oxidative stress drives the mitochondrial
injury and cellular death seen in severe toxicity.

question:
A 69-year-old man on warfarin presents with an intraparenchymal haemorrhage
on CT. He is conscious. His BP is 135/85 mmHg. What is the most important immediate step?

options.text: Administer mannitol for presumed high ICP.
Obtain a CT angiogram to look for an aneurysm.
Place an external ventricular drain (EVD).
Administer 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC).

Start an antihypertensive infusion.

Correct answerAdminister 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC).

correctAnswer: Administer 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC).
englishExplanation:
Immediate Reversal of Anticoagulation:
NICE NG36 and British Society for Haematology guidelines mandate immediate reversal of warfarin in primary intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH). The gold standard is
4-factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) combined with intravenous
Vitamin K (5 mg). PCC provides immediate replacement of factors II, VII, IX, and
X, while Vitamin K promotes sustained endogenous factor synthesis. This prevents
haematoma expansion, which is the primary driver of mortality.
Blood Pressure Management:
NICE NG36 recommends rapidly lowering systolic blood pressure to a target of 140
mmHg or lower within 1 hour for patients presenting within 6 hours of onset (provided SBP is between 150 and 220 mmHg). This patient has a BP of 135/85 mmHg,
which is already within the optimal target range. Therefore, starting an antihypertensive infusion (Option E) is unnecessary and potentially harmful if it induces
hypotension.
Other Interventions:
Mannitol (Option A) and EVD (Option C) are reserved for patients with clinical or
radiological evidence of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus; the patient
here is conscious. A CT angiogram (Option B) is useful for identifying secondary
causes (e.g., aneurysm) or the 'spot sign' (predicting expansion), but it must not delay life-saving reversal of coagulopathy.
Clinical Pearl
PCC + Vitamin K:
The standard reversal for warfarin-associated ICH is 4-factor PCC (25-50 units/kg)
plus IV Vitamin K (5 mg). PCC acts immediately, whereas Vitamin K takes 4-6
hours to effect INR.
FFP is Second Line:
Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) is inferior to PCC for urgent reversal. It requires thawing, large volumes (15-30 mL/kg) which may precipitate heart failure, and has lower
factor concentration. Use only if PCC is unavailable.
Blood Pressure Targets:
NICE NG36 recommends acute systolic blood pressure lowering to a target of 140
mmHg or lower within 1 hour of treatment initiation for patients with ICH, maintaining this for at least 7 days.
DOAC Reversal Agents:

Specific reversal agents are indicated for DOAC-associated ICH: Idarucizumab
(monoclonal antibody fragment) for Dabigatran, and Andexanet alfa (recombinant
decoy factor Xa) for Apixaban or Rivaroxaban.
Restarting Anticoagulation:
Avoid restarting anticoagulation acutely. NICE NG36 recommends a multidisciplinary review to consider restarting oral anticoagulation after 7 days, balancing the
risk of recurrent haemorrhage against thromboembolism.
Platelet Transfusion Contraindication:
Do not transfuse platelets for patients with spontaneous ICH on antiplatelet therapy
unless they have severe thrombocytopenia, as the PATCH trial demonstrated increased mortality and poor functional outcome with transfusion.
Warfarin Mechanism:
Warfarin inhibits Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), preventing the gammacarboxylation required for the activation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well
as Protein C and S.
INR Reversal Target:
The goal of reversal in warfarin-associated ICH is to achieve an INR < 1.5 immediately. Repeat INR testing is required after PCC administration to ensure the target is
maintained.
CT Angiography Spot Sign:
The 'spot sign' refers to the presence of contrast extravasation within a haematoma
on CT angiography. It is an independent predictor of haematoma expansion and
poor clinical outcome.

question:
A 65-year-old male presents with frequent, brief episodes of facial and arm
twitching lasting only a few seconds, occurring hundreds of times a day. He also
has worsening memory problems. An MRI shows hyperintensity in the medial
temporal lobes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Temporal lobe epilepsy
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
LGI1-antibody encephalitis
Frontotemporal dementia

Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis with anti-Hu antibodies

Correct answerLGI1-antibody encephalitis

correctAnswer: LGI1-antibody encephalitis
englishExplanation:
Diagnosis:
The combination of a specific and unusual seizure type with subacute cognitive decline and characteristic MRI findings is the classic presentation of LGI1-antibody
encephalitis.
Pathophysiology:
This is an autoimmune encephalitis where the body produces antibodies against the
Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 (LGI1) protein, a component of the voltage-gated
potassium channel complex in the brain. This antibody binding disrupts normal
synaptic function, particularly in the limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala).
Clinical Manifestations:
The two hallmark features are:
•1. Faciobrachial Dystonic Seizures (FBDS): These are pathognomonic
seizures. They are very frequent (often hundreds per day), very brief (<3 seconds),
and consist of a dystonic posturing of one arm and the ipsilateral face. They often
precede the onset of memory problems. •2. Limbic Encephalitis: This presents
with subacute memory loss, confusion, and other seizures. Hyponatremia (due to
SIADH) is also very common.
Radiological Findings:
The MRI often shows T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes, reflecting the limbic inflammation.
Analysis of Other Options:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) presents with rapidly progressive dementia and
myoclonus, but the jerks are typically startle-sensitive and not the frequent, spontaneous dystonic posturing of FBDS. MRI in CJD typically shows cortical ribboning or
basal ganglia hyperintensity rather than isolated medial temporal changes.
Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis with anti-Hu antibodies is strongly associated
with small cell lung cancer and often presents with sensory neuronopathy or cerebellar signs in addition to limbic encephalitis. Frontotemporal dementia involves atrophy rather than hyperintensity and presents with behavioural or language
deficits.
Clinical Pearl
FBDS is Pathognomonic:
If you see a description of frequent, brief, dystonic seizures affecting the face and
arm, the diagnosis is LGI1-antibody encephalitis until proven otherwise.

A Treatable Dementia:
This is an important diagnosis to make because, unlike degenerative dementias, it is
an autoimmune condition that is highly responsive to immunotherapy.
Hyponatremia is a Clue:
Hyponatraemia (SIADH) occurs in ~60% of patients. It is often refractory to fluid
restriction but resolves rapidly with immunotherapy.
Not Paraneoplastic:
LGI1-antibody encephalitis is rarely paraneoplastic (<10% association, usually thymoma). This contrasts with anti-NMDA (ovarian teratoma) or anti-Hu (SCLC)
encephalitis.
Treatment:
First-line treatment is with corticosteroids, IVIG, or plasmapheresis. Many patients
require long-term immunosuppression to prevent relapse.
The Prodromal Window:
FBDS often precede cognitive impairment by weeks. Early recognition and immunotherapy during this phase can prevent the development of permanent cognitive deficits (limbic encephalitis).
VGKC Complex Terminology:
LGI1 and CASPR2 antibodies were previously grouped as 'voltage-gated potassium
channel (VGKC) complex' antibodies. Modern testing distinguishes the specific
antigenic target, as the clinical phenotypes differ significantly.
CASPR2 Differential:
Anti-CASPR2 encephalitis presents differently to LGI1, often manifesting as
Morvan's syndrome (neuromyotonia, autonomic instability, and severe insomnia)
rather than the specific faciobrachial dystonic seizures of LGI1.
Anti-Epileptic Drug Resistance:
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures are characteristically resistant to standard antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) but respond rapidly and dramatically to corticosteroids.
Demographic Profile:
LGI1 encephalitis typically affects older males (median age 60), whereas antiNMDA receptor encephalitis predominantly affects younger females.

question:
All of the following statements about vasopressin receptor antagonists (e.g.,
tolvaptan) are correct EXCEPT:

options.text: They promote 'aquaresis,' which is the excretion of electrolyte-free water.

A primary indication is the treatment of euvolemic hyponatremia (e.g., SIADH)
where fluid restriction has failed.

By increasing free water excretion, they cause an increase in serum sodium
concentration.
They are known to cause significant hypokalemia due to their diuretic effect.

Their mechanism is to block V2 receptors in the renal collecting duct.

Correct answerThey are known to cause significant hypokalemia due to their diuretic effect.

correctAnswer: They are known to cause significant hypokalemia due to their diuretic effect.
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Tolvaptan is a selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist. By blocking V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of the renal collecting duct cells, it prevents the
insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane. This inhibits
free water reabsorption, resulting in 'aquaresis'—the excretion of electrolyte-free
water.
Electrolyte Handling:
Unlike loop diuretics (which block Na-K-2Cl cotransporters) or thiazides (which
block Na-Cl cotransporters), vaptans do not directly interfere with renal sodium or
potassium handling mechanisms. Therefore, they do not induce kaliuresis or significant hypokalaemia. The primary effect is an increase in serum sodium concentration due to the loss of free water.
Clinical Indications:
Tolvaptan is a selective V2 antagonist. In the UK and Europe, it is licensed specifically for the treatment of hyponatraemia secondary to SIADH (euvolemic hyponatraemia). Unlike in the United States, it is NOT licensed for hypervolemic hyponatraemia (heart failure or cirrhosis) in the UK. NICE TA358 recommends tolvaptan
for SIADH only if fluid restriction has failed or is not suitable. The European Society
of Endocrinology guidelines generally recommend against vaptans in hypervolemic
states.
Clinical Pearl
Aquaresis vs Diuresis:
Vaptans induce aquaresis (electrolyte-free water excretion) rather than natriuresis
(sodium excretion), distinguishing them from loop and thiazide diuretics.
UK Licensing Constraints:
In the UK and Europe, tolvaptan is licensed specifically for euvolemic hyponatraemia (SIADH) and is not licensed for hypervolemic hyponatraemia (heart failure
or cirrhosis), unlike in the US.
Osmotic Demyelination Risk:
Rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia can lead to osmotic demyelination syndrome. Serum sodium should not rise by more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24
hours.
Administration Route:

Tolvaptan is an oral agent. Intravenous vaptans (e.g., conivaptan) are not licensed
in the UK.
Volume Status Contraindication:
Vaptans are contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatraemia as they worsen volume
depletion.
Hepatotoxicity Monitoring:
Tolvaptan carries a risk of idiosyncratic liver injury. Liver function tests are required before and during treatment; duration is often limited to minimize risk.
Thirst Mechanism Prerequisite:
Patients must have an intact thirst mechanism and access to water to prevent severe
hypernatraemia and dehydration during aquaresis.
CYP3A4 Interactions:
Tolvaptan is a CYP3A4 substrate. Co-administration with inhibitors (e.g., clarithromycin, ketoconazole) or inducers (e.g., rifampicin) requires caution or
avoidance.
Comparison with Demeclocycline:
Demeclocycline is a tetracycline antibiotic that induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus to treat SIADH but has a slower onset (days) and variable efficacy compared
to vaptans.
Monitoring Frequency:
Due to the unpredictable rate of aquaresis, serum sodium should be monitored frequently (e.g., every 4-6 hours) during initiation to prevent overcorrection.

question: An 18-month-old child is admitted after an accidental ingestion of oil of wintergreen (methyl salicylate). The child is hyperthermic, tachypneic, and has an altered mental status. Which acid-base disturbance is the dominant and most characteristic finding in a young child with salicylate poisoning?

options.text: A primary respiratory alkalosis only.
A mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis.
A primary, severe metabolic acidosis.
A primary metabolic alkalosis.

A primary respiratory acidosis.

Correct answerA primary, severe metabolic acidosis.

correctAnswer: A primary, severe metabolic acidosis.
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
Salicylates act via two primary mechanisms: direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory centre (causing respiratory alkalosis) and uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria. This uncoupling halts aerobic metabolism, forcing a
switch to anaerobic glycolysis (producing lactate) and lipid metabolism (producing
ketones). Additionally, salicylic acid itself is a weak acid.
In adults, the respiratory drive is robust, classically resulting in a mixed respiratory
alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. However, in infants and young children (typically
under 4 years), the metabolic toxicity develops rapidly. The accumulation of lactate,
ketoacids, and salicylate overwhelms the respiratory compensatory reserve.
Consequently, the dominant presentation in toddlers is a severe high anion gap
metabolic acidosis. The initial respiratory alkalosis phase is often transient or
missed entirely before presentation.
Clinical Pearl
Paediatric Acid-Base Presentation:
The classic teaching distinguishes age groups: adults typically present with a mixed
respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, whereas young children (<4 years) predominantly present with a severe primary metabolic acidosis.
Methyl Salicylate Potency:
Methyl salicylate is highly concentrated. 5mL (one teaspoon) of Oil of Wintergreen
contains approximately 7g of salicylate, equivalent to ~21 adult aspirin tablets
(300mg each). This is a potentially lethal dose for a toddler.
Sepsis Mimicry:
Salicylate poisoning presents with fever (hyperthermia from uncoupling), tachypnoea, altered mental status, and metabolic acidosis. This constellation of signs is
easily misdiagnosed as severe sepsis or meningitis in a child.
Urinary Alkalinisation:
Urinary alkalinisation (ion trapping) is the mainstay of treatment for moderate toxicity. The goal is a urine pH of 7.5–8.5. Alkalinity converts salicylic acid (HA) to its
ionised form (A-), which is impermeable to the tubule membrane, preventing reabsorption and enhancing excretion.
Indications for Haemodialysis:

Haemodialysis is the definitive treatment for severe poisoning. Indications include
severe acidosis (pH <7.20), refractory hypotension, renal failure, CNS toxicity
(seizures, coma), pulmonary oedema, or very high serum levels (>7.2 mmol/L or
100 mg/dL acute).
Hypokalaemia and Alkalinisation:
Effective urinary alkalinisation is impossible in the presence of hypokalaemia. The
kidneys will preferentially reabsorb potassium in exchange for secreting hydrogen
ions (paradoxical aciduria) to maintain serum potassium. Aggressive potassium replacement is required.
Neuroglycopenia Risk:
Salicylates uncouple oxidative phosphorylation and increase cerebral metabolic demand. CNS glucose levels may be low despite normal serum glucose; maintain
serum glucose in the high-normal range.
Intubation Hazards:
Intubation is extremely high risk. The patient relies on massive respiratory compensation (high minute volume) to maintain pH. The apnoea associated with induction
causes a rapid rise in PaCO2, precipitating severe acidaemia. This shifts salicylate
into the non-ionised form, facilitating entry into the CNS and potentially causing
cardiac arrest.
Acetazolamide Contraindication:
Acetazolamide must be avoided. While it alkalinises the urine, it causes systemic
metabolic acidosis. This acidaemia shifts the equilibrium of salicylate towards the
non-ionised, lipophilic form, increasing penetration into the brain and worsening
toxicity.
Hyperthermia Mechanism:
Hyperthermia is a grave prognostic sign. It results from the uncoupling of oxidative
phosphorylation in the mitochondria; energy that would normally produce ATP is
instead dissipated as heat.
Gastric Decontamination:
Activated charcoal is effective if given early (within 1 hour). For massive ingestions
or enteric-coated preparations, multi-dose activated charcoal is often recommended
as salicylates can form concretions (bezoars) in the stomach, leading to delayed or
prolonged absorption.

question:
Which statement accurately describes the pharmacokinetics of the anti-epileptic
drug levetiracetam?

options.text: It is extensively metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes.
It has a very low oral bioavailability.
The majority of the drug is excreted unchanged in the urine.
It is a potent inducer of hepatic enzymes.

Its clearance is primarily dependent on liver function.

Correct answerThe majority of the drug is excreted unchanged in the urine.

correctAnswer: The majority of the drug is excreted unchanged in the urine.
englishExplanation:
General Pharmacokinetics:
Levetiracetam exhibits linear pharmacokinetics with low protein binding (<10%). It
is not metabolised by the hepatic cytochrome P450 system, resulting in a minimal
risk of drug-drug interactions compared to older anti-epileptics.
Metabolism and Excretion:
The major route of elimination is renal excretion of unchanged drug (approximately
66% of the dose). The remainder undergoes enzymatic hydrolysis (not hepatic
CYP450) in the blood and tissues to an inactive metabolite. Total body clearance is
directly related to creatinine clearance.
Bioavailability:
Oral bioavailability is nearly 100%, allowing for a convenient 1:1 conversion between intravenous and oral formulations.
Mechanism of Action:
Levetiracetam binds to the synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A), a glycoprotein involved in the regulation of vesicle exocytosis. This binding modulates the release of
neurotransmitters (including glutamate) into the synaptic cleft, reducing neuronal
hyperexcitability. This mechanism is distinct from sodium channel blockers (e.g.,
phenytoin) or GABA-ergic agents.
Clinical Pearl
Pharmacokinetic Profile:
Levetiracetam has minimal hepatic metabolism and a low drug-drug interaction potential, making it safer than older agents in complex polypharmacy.
Dose-Adjust for Renal Function:
Dosing requires adjustment based on creatinine clearance (CrCl). For example, frequency reduces to every 12-24 hours or dose decreases as CrCl drops below 50-80
ml/min.
No CYP Interactions:
This is a major advantage over older anti-epileptics like phenytoin, carbamazepine,
and valproic acid.
Behavioural Side Effects:
The most common side effects are somnolence, dizziness, and behavioural changes,
including irritability and agitation ('Keppra-rage').
Broad Spectrum of Activity:

Levetiracetam is effective for both focal and generalised seizures, making it a widely
used first-line agent.
IV to Oral Conversion:
Due to >95% bioavailability, the conversion ratio from IV to oral dosing is 1:1, facilitating easy step-down from critical care.
Dialysis Considerations:
Levetiracetam is significantly removed by haemodialysis (~50% extraction efficiency). A supplemental dose is required immediately after a dialysis session.
Status Epilepticus Dosing:
NICE NG217 recommends a loading dose of 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg) for status epilepticus if established treatment fails.
Mechanism of Action:
Levetiracetam binds to synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A), modulating neurotransmitter release. This unique mechanism distinguishes it from traditional sodium
channel blockers or GABA enhancers.
Pregnancy Considerations:
Levetiracetam has a lower teratogenic risk compared to valproate. However, physiological changes in pregnancy significantly increase renal clearance, often necessitating dose increases and monitoring of levels.
Therapeutic Drug Monitoring:
Routine monitoring is not required due to linear pharmacokinetics and a wide therapeutic index. However, levels may be useful in pregnancy, renal failure, or suspected non-adherence.

question:
An arterial line tracing from a patient with severe, end-stage cardiomyopathy
shows a beat-to-beat alternation in the height of the systolic pressure, which is
not related to the respiratory cycle. What is this sign, and what does it signify?

options.text: Pulsus paradoxus; suggests cardiac tamponade.
Pulsus bisferiens; suggests aortic regurgitation.
Pulsus alternans; suggests severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction.
Dicrotic pulse; suggests a low cardiac output state.

A measurement artifact.

Correct answerPulsus alternans; suggests severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

correctAnswer: Pulsus alternans; suggests severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction.
englishExplanation:
Definition:
Pulsus alternans is the physical sign of a beat-to-beat alternation in the stroke volume and systolic pressure, independent of respiration.
Pathophysiology:
The mechanism involves intracellular calcium handling dysfunction in the failing
myocardium. Alternating sequestration and release of calcium by the sarcoplasmic
reticulum leads to beat-to-beat variation in myocardial contractility (inotropy) despite constant end-diastolic volume and heart rate.
Clinical Significance:
It is a specific but insensitive sign of severe, end-stage left ventricular systolic dysfunction. The presence of pulsus alternans is a very poor prognostic sign, indicating
that the ventricle has exhausted its contractile reserve.
Differentiation from Bigeminy:
Pulsus alternans must be distinguished from pulsus bigeminus (bigeminy). In
bigeminy, the alternation in pulse volume is due to alternating coupling intervals
(short-long R-R intervals). In pulsus alternans, the rhythm is regular (constant R-R
intervals) but the force varies.
Clinical Pearl
Waveform Morphology:
The hallmark is a regular rhythm with alternating strong and weak systolic peaks on
the arterial waveform, independent of the respiratory cycle.
Prognostic Implications:
The presence of pulsus alternans is a very poor prognostic sign, indicating that the
ventricle has exhausted its contractile reserve.
Detection Methods:
It is most easily seen on an arterial line tracing. It can sometimes be detected by
sphygmomanometry, where the Korotkoff sounds will be heard at every other beat
over a certain pressure range.
Distinction from Electrical Alternans:
Do not confuse pulsus alternans (alternation of pressure) with electrical alternans
(alternation of QRS amplitude), which is a sign of pericardial effusion.
Clinical Severity:
Pulsus alternans often precedes the development of cardiogenic shock or cardiovascular collapse.

Differentiation from Bigeminy:
To distinguish Pulsus Alternans from Pulsus Bigeminus (ventricular bigeminy), look
at the ECG. Pulsus Alternans occurs in normal sinus rhythm (regular R-R intervals).
Bigeminy shows alternating short and long R-R intervals.
Pathophysiological Mechanism:
While historically attributed to the Frank-Starling mechanism (alternating end-diastolic volumes), current evidence suggests the primary driver is alternating intracellular calcium cycling in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Distinction from Pulsus Paradoxus:
Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggeration of the normal inspiratory drop in systolic pressure (>10 mmHg). Pulsus alternans is a beat-to-beat variation unrelated to the respiratory phase.
Associated Conditions:
Pulsus alternans is most commonly associated with dilated cardiomyopathy, but can
also be seen in severe aortic stenosis and rapid supraventricular tachycardias.
Auscultatory Findings:
The condition is frequently associated with a third heart sound (S3 gallop), reinforcing the diagnosis of severe ventricular failure.

question:
A patient with G6PD deficiency is given methylene blue for refractory vasoplegic
shock. They subsequently develop a precipitous drop in their hemoglobin and
jaundice. This hemolytic crisis is caused by what property of methylene blue?

options.text: Methylene blue is a direct immunosuppressant.

Methylene blue is a potent oxidising agent in the absence of a functional pentose
