Caspofungin inhibits 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase, disrupting the fungal cell wall.
This target is absent in mammalian cells, contributing to the low side-effect profile
compared to azoles or amphotericin.
Azole Mechanism:
Azoles inhibit 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis. This enzyme is a
cytochrome P450 equivalent, explaining the high potential for drug-drug interactions via human CYP inhibition.
Voriconazole Toxicity:
Unique side effects of voriconazole include transient visual disturbances (photopsia), phototoxicity (skin rash), and with long-term use, fluoride excess leading to
periostitis.
Therapeutic Drug Monitoring:
TDM is frequently required for itraconazole, voriconazole, and posaconazole due to
variable bioavailability and non-linear pharmacokinetics (voriconazole).
Echinocandins do not require TDM.
Posaconazole Formulations:
Posaconazole oral suspension requires a high-fat meal for adequate absorption,
whereas the delayed-release tablet and IV formulations do not. This is critical in enterally fed ICU patients.

question:
An ICU patient develops a CRBSI. Blood cultures from the catheter and a peripheral site both grow Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which empiric antibiotic should be
initiated while awaiting sensitivity results?

options.text: Vancomycin
Ceftriaxone
Piperacillin/tazobactam
Amoxicillin

Clindamycin

Correct answerPiperacillin/tazobactam

correctAnswer: Piperacillin/tazobactam
englishExplanation:
Analysis of the Correct Answer:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative non-fermenter with intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics. Piperacillin/tazobactam is an antipseudomonal penicillin
and the only option listed with reliable activity against this pathogen. It is a standard first-line therapy in UK practice for suspected or confirmed Pseudomonas infections pending susceptibility testing.
Analysis of Other Options:
Vancomycin (Glycopeptide) and Clindamycin (Lincosamide) cover Gram-positive
organisms and anaerobes but have no activity against Gram-negatives like
Pseudomonas. Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin with broad Gramnegative coverage but specifically lacks activity against Pseudomonas. Amoxicillin is
an aminopenicillin with no activity against Pseudomonas.
Alternative Agents:
Other agents with anti-pseudomonal activity include Ceftazidime (3rd gen
cephalosporin), Cefepime (4th gen cephalosporin), Carbapenems (Meropenem,
Imipenem), Aztreonam, Ciprofloxacin, and Aminoglycosides (Gentamicin,
Amikacin, Tobramycin).
Clinical Pearl
Remove the Catheter:
Catheter removal is mandatory for CRBSI caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, S.
aureus, and Candida spp. Attempting to salvage the line with antibiotic locks is generally not recommended for these pathogens due to high failure and recurrence
rates.
Double-Cover for Sepsis:
Combination therapy (e.g., beta-lactam + aminoglycoside) is recommended for
Pseudomonas bacteremia in patients with neutropenia or septic shock to increase
the likelihood of initial adequate coverage. Once susceptibilities are known and the
patient stabilizes, de-escalation to monotherapy is standard.
Anti-Pseudomonal Cephalosporins:
Ceftazidime and Cefepime are the only cephalosporins with reliable anti-pseudomonal activity. Ceftriaxone and Cefotaxime do NOT cover Pseudomonas.
Duration of Therapy:
For uncomplicated Pseudomonas CRBSI where the line is removed, treatment duration is typically 7-14 days. Longer courses (4-6 weeks) are required for complicated

infections (e.g., endocarditis, osteomyelitis, persistent bacteraemia >72h after line
removal).
Follow-up Blood Cultures:
Repeat blood cultures should be obtained after initiation of appropriate therapy and
catheter removal to document clearance of bacteraemia, as persistent positivity suggests metastatic foci or endocarditis.
Ertapenem Exception:
While meropenem and imipenem have excellent anti-pseudomonal activity, ertapenem does NOT cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This is a critical distinction
when selecting carbapenems for empiric therapy in patients with risk factors for
Pseudomonas.
Oral Step-down Options:
Ciprofloxacin is the only oral antibiotic with reliable anti-pseudomonal bioavailability (approximately 70-80%). It is the agent of choice for oral step-down therapy
once susceptibility is confirmed. Levofloxacin has variable activity and moxifloxacin
has no anti-pseudomonal activity.
Tazobactam Pharmacology:
In piperacillin/tazobactam, the anti-pseudomonal effect is derived almost entirely
from piperacillin. Tazobactam inhibits Class A beta-lactamases (common in
Enterobacteriaceae) but has limited activity against the chromosomal AmpC betalactamases or efflux pumps that typically mediate Pseudomonas resistance.
Intrinsic Resistance Profile:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa possesses intrinsic resistance to ampicillin, amoxicillinclavulanate, first and second-generation cephalosporins, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime,
ertapenem, and tigecycline. This resistance is mediated by low outer membrane permeability (porins) and constitutive expression of efflux pumps.
Ecthyma Gangrenosum:
This is a pathognomonic cutaneous lesion of Pseudomonas bacteraemia, typically
seen in immunocompromised patients. It presents as a painless, red macule that
rapidly evolves into a haemorrhagic bulla and then a necrotic ulcer with a black eschar, caused by perivascular bacterial invasion.

question:
An elderly man presents with an acute inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. On examination, his blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg, his jugular veins are
distended, and his lung fields are clear on auscultation. Which medication is absolutely contraindicated in this setting?

options.text: Aspirin
A cautious intravenous fluid bolus
Nitroglycerin
An urgent primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)

A norepinephrine infusion

Correct answerNitroglycerin

correctAnswer: Nitroglycerin
englishExplanation:
Diagnosis:
The clinical triad of hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and clear lungs
in the setting of an inferior MI is classic for a right ventricular (RV) infarction.
Pathophysiology:
In RV infarction, the right ventricle becomes stiff, non-compliant, and stunned. It
fails to pump blood effectively into the pulmonary circulation, becoming highly dependent on high central venous pressure (preload) to drive blood flow passively
through the pulmonary vasculature to the left heart. Additionally, acute RV dilation
can shift the interventricular septum toward the left ventricle (ventricular interdependence), impairing LV filling and further reducing cardiac output.
Pharmacological Contraindications:
Nitroglycerin (and other nitrates) acts as a potent venodilator, significantly reducing venous return (preload). In a preload-dependent RV, this causes a precipitous
drop in cardiac output and severe hypotension. It is contraindicated in patients with
systolic BP <90 mmHg or suspected RV infarction.
Management Strategy:
Initial management involves cautious fluid resuscitation to optimize RV preload. If
hypotension persists despite fluid loading, vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) are
indicated to maintain coronary perfusion pressure. Inotropic support may be required if cardiac output remains low.
Clinical Pearl
Hypotension + JVD + Clear Lungs:
This is the classic triad for an RV infarct.
Right-Sided ECG:
Obtain a right-sided ECG in all inferior STEMIs. ST-elevation of at least 1 mm in
lead V4R is the single most sensitive and specific ECG sign of RV infarction.
No Nitrates, No Morphine, No Beta-Blockers:
Avoid preload-reducing agents (nitrates, opioids, diuretics) and negative
inotropes/chronotropes (beta-blockers) in the acute phase. These can precipitate
profound shock in a preload-dependent, stunned RV.
Inferior MI is the Context:
Maintain a high index of suspicion: RV infarction complicates approximately 3050% of inferior wall STEMIs.
Reperfusion is Definitive:

The ultimate treatment is to open the occluded right coronary artery with primary
PCI, which will restore blood flow to the RV and allow it to recover function.
Anatomical Correlation:
RV infarction typically results from occlusion of the proximal Right Coronary Artery
(RCA), proximal to the acute marginal branch which supplies the RV free wall.
Fluid Resuscitation Limits:
While fluid is first-line, avoid over-distension. If there is no response after 5001000 mL of crystalloid, initiate vasopressors. Excessive fluid can shift the interventricular septum (ventricular interdependence), impairing LV filling and worsening
cardiac output.
Atrial Dependence:
The stiff, ischemic RV is highly dependent on atrial contraction for filling. The onset
of atrial fibrillation can precipitate hemodynamic collapse and often requires urgent
cardioversion.
Bezold-Jarisch Reflex:
Stimulation of vagal afferents in the inferior LV wall can cause profound bradycardia and vasodilation. This often responds to atropine, though volume resuscitation
and temporary pacing may be required.
Echocardiographic Signs:
Look for RV dilatation, hypokinesis, and septal flattening (D-shaped left ventricle)
during systole, indicating RV pressure overload and ventricular interdependence.
V4R Lead Placement:
To obtain V4R, place the V4 electrode in the 5th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line on the right chest wall. This should be routine for all inferior STEMI
presentations.

question:
The "Lethal Triad" of trauma-induced coagulopathy is classically described as
Acidosis, Hypothermia, and Coagulopathy. Modern damage control resuscitation
has identified a fourth, critical component, creating the "Lethal Diamond." What
is this fourth component?

options.text: Hyperglycemia
Hypocalcemia
Hyperkalemia
Anemia

Inflammation

Correct answerHypocalcemia

correctAnswer: Hypocalcemia
englishExplanation:
The Lethal Diamond:
The classic 'Lethal Triad' (acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy) has been expanded
to the 'Lethal Diamond' to include hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia in trauma is multifactorial, resulting from citrate chelation during massive transfusion, dilution, and
ischemia-reperfusion injury. Ionized calcium (Factor IV) is a mandatory cofactor for
the assembly of coagulation complexes (tenase and prothrombinase) on phospholipid surfaces. The European Guideline on Management of Major Bleeding and
Coagulopathy Following Trauma recommends monitoring ionized calcium levels
during major trauma resuscitation and maintaining them within the normal range
to prevent coagulopathy and myocardial depression.
Clinical Pearl
Lethal Diamond Components:
The modern 'Lethal Diamond' concept adds hypocalcaemia to the classic triad of
acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy, recognising its independent contribution
to mortality.
Monitoring Targets:
Monitor ionised calcium levels frequently during massive haemorrhage. European
Trauma Guidelines suggest maintaining levels within the normal range (typically
>1.1 mmol/L), as levels <0.9 mmol/L are associated with significantly increased
mortality.
Calcium Replacement Strategy:
Administer calcium chloride (preferred in arrest/severe shock due to immediate
ionisation) or calcium gluconate during massive transfusion. A common pragmatic
ratio is 10ml of 10% Calcium Chloride for every 4 units of blood products, though
guided replacement is superior.
Impact on Coagulopathy:
Hypocalcaemia is a critical, often iatrogenic, and easily correctable driver of
trauma-induced coagulopathy.
Citrate Chelation Mechanism:
Citrate used as an anticoagulant in blood products chelates ionised calcium, leading
to functional hypocalcaemia. This effect is exacerbated when liver clearance of citrate is impaired by shock or hypothermia.
Factor IV Function:

Calcium is historically known as Factor IV. It acts as a bridge binding clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) to the phospholipid surface of platelets, facilitating the formation of the tenase and prothrombinase complexes.
Admission Hypocalcemia:
Hypocalcemia is not solely iatrogenic; up to 50% of major trauma patients present
with hypocalcemia on admission before transfusion, which is an independent predictor of mortality and need for massive transfusion.
Myocardial Depression:
Severe hypocalcaemia causes negative inotropy and vasoplegia, which can manifest
as hypotension refractory to vasopressors. Correction of calcium is essential for
haemodynamic stability.
ECG Manifestations:
The classic ECG change associated with hypocalcaemia is QTc prolongation, which
can predispose to Torsades de Pointes, although this is rare in the acute trauma setting compared to electromechanical dissociation.
Citrate Metabolism:
Citrate is metabolised by the liver (Krebs cycle). In patients with severe liver
trauma, cirrhosis, or profound shock (liver hypoperfusion), citrate clearance is reduced, significantly increasing the risk of 'citrate lock' and profound hypocalcaemia.

question:
During ICP monitoring after traumatic brain injury, the monitor shows sustained
plateau elevations of ICP to 50-100 mmHg lasting 5-20 minutes. What are these
waves called, and what is their significance?

options.text: Lundberg B waves - benign and of no significance

Lundberg A (plateau) waves - pathological, indicating critically reduced
compliance
Traube-Hering waves - reflecting normal blood pressure oscillation
Dicrotic waves - a normal arterial reflection
Lundberg C waves - normal respiratory variation

correctAnswer:
Lundberg A (plateau) waves - pathological, indicating critically reduced
compliance
englishExplanation:
Lundberg A waves, or plateau waves, are sustained elevations of intracranial pressure, classically to approximately 50-100 mmHg for about 5-20 minutes. They indicate markedly reduced intracranial compensatory reserve and are accompanied by
reductions in cerebral perfusion pressure and cerebral blood flow. They are pathological and require urgent assessment and treatment, but an individual wave should
not be described as proof that herniation is inevitably imminent. B waves are
shorter slow oscillations that can also be associated with disturbed intracranial dynamics; C waves are smaller, faster oscillations of limited clinical importance.
Clinical Pearl
A (Plateau) Waves:
These are abrupt, sustained rises in intracranial pressure, classically reaching about
50-100 mmHg for 5-20 minutes.
Pathophysiology:
They arise from cerebral vasodilatory cascades when intracranial compensatory reserve is severely reduced.
Perfusion Consequence:
The rise in intracranial pressure can markedly reduce cerebral perfusion pressure
and cerebral blood flow.
Clinical Significance:
Plateau waves are pathological and can accompany transient neurological deterioration, but they do not prove that herniation is inevitable.
B Waves:
B waves are slower recurrent oscillations whose significance depends on pattern
and clinical context; they are not always benign.
C Waves:
C waves are smaller, faster oscillations related to systemic vasomotor activity and
generally have limited clinical significance.
Urgent Response:
Assess the patient and waveform, exclude artefact, optimise cerebral perfusion and
treat raised intracranial pressure according to the underlying cause.
Termination:
A plateau wave commonly ends with a relatively rapid fall in intracranial pressure
as the vasodilatory cascade reverses.

question:
A 58-year-old man with decompensated heart failure is started on levosimendan.
What is its principal inotropic mechanism of action?

options.text: Direct L-type calcium channel activation
Beta-1 adrenoceptor agonism increasing cyclic AMP
Calcium sensitisation via binding to cardiac troponin C
Selective phosphodiesterase-5 inhibition

Inhibition of the sarcolemmal sodium-potassium ATPase

Correct answerCalcium sensitisation via binding to cardiac troponin C

correctAnswer: Calcium sensitisation via binding to cardiac troponin C
englishExplanation:
Levosimendan's principal inotropic action is calcium sensitisation: it binds to cardiac troponin C in a calcium-dependent manner and increases myofilament responsiveness to calcium. It also opens vascular ATP-sensitive potassium channels, producing systemic and pulmonary vasodilation, and PDE3 inhibition may contribute
to its effects, particularly at higher concentrations. Opening of mitochondrial potassium channels has been proposed as a cardioprotective mechanism, but this should
not be treated as a proven clinical outcome.
Clinical Pearl
Calcium Sensitisation:
Levosimendan increases the calcium sensitivity of troponin C and thereby enhances
contraction.
Inodilator:
Opening of vascular ATP-sensitive potassium channels produces systemic and pulmonary vasodilation as well as inotropy.
PDE3 Contribution:
PDE3 inhibition may contribute, especially at higher concentrations, so the drug is
not pharmacologically a pure calcium sensitiser.
Oxygen-Demand Profile:
It may increase contractility with less direct calcium loading than catecholamines,
but it should not be assumed to be free of myocardial oxygen or arrhythmic
consequences.
Adverse Effects:
Hypotension, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmias can occur.
Mitochondrial Hypothesis:
Mitochondrial potassium-channel opening has been proposed to confer cellular
protection, but a definite clinical cardioprotective benefit is unproven.
Preload and Pressure:
Correct hypovolaemia and monitor blood pressure closely because vasodilation can
cause clinically important hypotension.
Outcome Evidence:
Haemodynamic improvement does not translate into a consistent mortality benefit
in acute decompensated heart failure.

question:
A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation with a known history of Marfan syndrome presents with acute, tearing chest pain. Her blood pressure is 160/70
mmHg in the right arm and 120/50 mmHg in the left. A Stanford Type A aortic
dissection is suspected. Which statement regarding this condition in pregnancy is
most accurate?

options.text: Medical management with beta-blockers is the preferred treatment to avoid surgical risk to the fetus.

The diagnosis should be confirmed with a CT angiogram due to its speed and
accuracy.
The risk of aortic dissection is highest in the first trimester of pregnancy.

Urgent surgical repair is indicated, with cardiopulmonary bypass and delivery of
the fetus via caesarean section often performed concurrently.
Uncontrolled hypertension is the most common underlying risk factor for dissection in this population.

correctAnswer:
Urgent surgical repair is indicated, with cardiopulmonary bypass and delivery of
the fetus via caesarean section often performed concurrently.
englishExplanation:
Surgical Urgency:
Stanford Type A aortic dissection is a catastrophic event requiring immediate surgical repair to prevent rupture and death. Maternal mortality increases by 1-2% per
hour without intervention. Pregnancy does not alter the indication for urgent
surgery.
Obstetric Management:
Management of the fetus depends on gestational age. At >28-32 weeks (viable), the
standard of care is Caesarean section immediately followed by aortic repair (or performed during cooling/bypass initiation). This optimizes fetal survival before the
deleterious effects of cardiopulmonary bypass (hypothermia, non-pulsatile flow,
placental hypoperfusion). For pre-viable fetuses (<24 weeks), aortic repair is performed with the fetus in utero, though fetal mortality remains high.
Diagnostic Imaging:
While CT angiography (CTA) is the gold standard in non-pregnant patients,
Transoesophageal Echocardiography (TOE) is often preferred in pregnancy to avoid
ionizing radiation, provided it does not delay definitive treatment. However, if TOE
is unavailable or expertise is lacking, CTA should not be withheld due to radiation
concerns given the immediate threat to maternal life.
Epidemiology and Pathophysiology:
The risk of dissection peaks in the third trimester and the immediate postpartum
period due to hypervolaemia and hormonal effects on the vasculature. In women
under 40, connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, Ehlers-Danlos IV) are
the most common underlying risk factor, accounting for up to 50% of cases. Marfan
syndrome involves a mutation in the Fibrillin-1 gene, leading to cystic medial degeneration. This structural weakness is exacerbated by the haemodynamic stress of
pregnancy (increased stroke volume) and hormonal changes
(oestrogen/progesterone) that further weaken the aortic media.
Clinical Pearl
Type A = Always Surgery:
This is a non-negotiable principle of cardiovascular emergencies.
Marfan + Pregnancy = High Risk:
Women with Marfan syndrome and a dilated aortic root require extensive pre-conception counseling and very close monitoring during pregnancy.

TOE in Instability:
In a haemodynamically unstable pregnant patient, a transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) in the operating room is the fastest and safest diagnostic test, avoiding
radiation to the fetus.
Anti-Impulse Therapy Targets:
In the acute phase prior to surgery, strict blood pressure control is vital. Aim for a
systolic BP of 100-120 mmHg and a heart rate <60 bpm. IV Labetalol is the firstline agent in pregnancy; Sodium Nitroprusside should be used with caution due to
potential fetal thiocyanate toxicity.
The 28-Week Threshold:
Gestational age dictates the surgical sequence. Before 28 weeks, the uterus is usually left intact during repair (unless fetal distress/death mandates delivery). After 32
weeks, concomitant Caesarean section is standard. The 28-32 week window is a
'grey zone' requiring individualised MDT decision-making.
Postpartum Danger Zone:
The risk of dissection does not end at delivery. The immediate postpartum period
involves significant haemodynamic shifts (autotransfusion from the contracting
uterus), maintaining a high risk for dissection or rupture in susceptible patients.
Radiation Risk Perspective:
Maternal survival is the absolute priority. Do not delay a CT aortogram if TTE/TOE
is inconclusive or unavailable. The radiation dose from a CT chest is generally below
the threshold for fetal deterministic effects, especially in the third trimester.
Marfan Pathophysiology:
Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the Fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1), which
leads to defective microfibrils and dysregulation of TGF-beta signalling. This results
in cystic medial necrosis/degeneration, weakening the aortic wall and predisposing
it to dissection.
Pregnancy-Induced Vascular Changes:
Pregnancy increases dissection risk through two mechanisms: haemodynamic stress
(50% increase in blood volume and cardiac output) and hormonal effects (relaxin,
oestrogen, and progesterone) which decrease the collagen/elastin content of the
aortic media.

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical characteristic of pressure control ventilation (PCV)?

options.text: A preset inspiratory pressure is delivered.
The inspiratory flow waveform is decelerating.
It often improves patient-ventilator synchrony compared to volume control.
The delivered tidal volume is constant with each breath.

The pressure waveform shows a square shape.

Correct answerThe delivered tidal volume is constant with each breath.

correctAnswer: The delivered tidal volume is constant with each breath.
englishExplanation:
Fundamental Principles:
The defining characteristic of Pressure Control Ventilation (PCV) is that the inspiratory pressure is the independent variable set by the clinician, while tidal volume is
the dependent variable. This contrasts with Volume Control Ventilation (VCV),
where tidal volume is set and pressure varies based on lung mechanics.
Waveform Characteristics:
In PCV, the ventilator rapidly pressurizes the circuit to the preset level and holds it
for the inspiratory time, generating a 'square' or rectangular pressure waveform. To
maintain this constant pressure as the alveoli fill, the flow is initially high and then
tapers off, creating a decelerating flow waveform.
Clinical Implications and Physiology:
Because tidal volume is not fixed in PCV, it varies according to the Equation of
Motion: Pressure = (Flow x Resistance) + (Volume / Compliance). Since the
Pressure is fixed by the clinician, any decrease in Compliance (stiffer lungs) or increase in Resistance (bronchospasm) must result in a lower delivered Volume. This
necessitates careful monitoring of minute ventilation to detect changes in lung mechanics. In contrast, Option D describes Volume Control, where tidal volume is constant regardless of mechanics.
Clinical Pearl
PCV = Set Pressure, Variable Volume:
In PCV, pressure is the independent (set) variable, while flow and volume are dependent variables determined by the patient's mechanics (compliance and
resistance).
VCV = Set Volume, Variable Pressure:
In VCV, the tidal volume is guaranteed (independent variable), but the resulting airway pressure varies based on lung compliance and airway resistance.
Decelerating Flow:
The decelerating flow pattern in PCV is thought to be more physiological and may
lead to better gas distribution and lower peak pressures compared to the constant
flow in VCV.
Risk of Hypo/Hyperventilation:
Because the tidal volume is not guaranteed in PCV, it is crucial to set alarms for low
and high minute ventilation to detect changes in the patient's lung mechanics.
Synchrony:

PCV often improves synchrony by matching patient inspiratory demand with variable flow. VCV can cause 'flow starvation' if the patient's demand exceeds the fixed
flow setting.
Leak Compensation:
PCV compensates for system leaks (e.g., bronchopleural fistula, cuff leak) better
than VCV. The ventilator increases flow to maintain the set pressure despite the
leak, whereas VCV delivers a fixed volume regardless of loss.
Mean Airway Pressure:
Due to the square pressure waveform, PCV typically achieves a higher mean airway
pressure than VCV for the same peak inspiratory pressure, which may improve oxygenation in hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
Equation of Motion:
The governing physical principle is: Pressure = (Flow x Resistance) + (Volume /
Compliance). In PCV, Pressure is constant. Therefore, Volume is directly proportional to Compliance and inversely proportional to Resistance.
Cycling Variable Distinction:
PCV is time-cycled (inspiration ends after a set inspiratory time), whereas Pressure
Support Ventilation (PSV) is flow-cycled (inspiration ends when inspiratory flow
drops to a specific percentage of peak flow, typically 25%).
Rise Time Adjustment:
Rise time determines how quickly the ventilator reaches the set target pressure. A
rise time that is too fast may cause pressure overshoot and patient discomfort, while
a rise time that is too slow increases the work of breathing and reduces the time
available for gas exchange.
Inverse Ratio Ventilation:
PCV facilitates inverse ratio ventilation (I:E ratio > 1:1) more easily than VCV. This
strategy increases mean airway pressure to recruit alveoli in severe ARDS but usually requires heavy sedation and neuromuscular blockade.
Peak vs Plateau Pressure:
In PCV, the set inspiratory pressure (plus PEEP) approximates the plateau pressure
if the flow waveform returns to zero before exhalation begins. In VCV, there is often
a significant difference between Peak Pressure (overcoming resistance + elastance)
and Plateau Pressure (overcoming elastance only).

question:
All of the following are potential causes of Right Axis Deviation (RAD) on an ECG
EXCEPT:

options.text: Left posterior fascicular block
Lateral myocardial infarction
Right ventricular hypertrophy
Acute pulmonary embolism

Left bundle branch block

Correct answerLeft bundle branch block

correctAnswer:
Left bundle branch block

Correct answerLeft bundle branch block
englishExplanation:
Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB):
LBBB is classically associated with Left Axis Deviation (LAD) or a normal axis. The
delayed depolarisation of the left ventricle results in a net electrical vector directed
towards the left and posteriorly. It is not a cause of Right Axis Deviation (RAD).
Causes of Right Axis Deviation:
RAD (axis > +90°) occurs when electrical forces shift rightward. Mechanisms
include:
•Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH): Increased muscle mass on the right
generates stronger vectors. •Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Acute right
ventricular strain/dilatation. •Left Posterior Fascicular Block (LPFB):
Delayed activation of the posterior-inferior LV shifts the axis rightward. •Lateral
Myocardial Infarction: Loss of electrical forces in the lateral wall (Leads I, aVL)
shifts the mean vector away from the infarction, towards the right.
Clinical Pearl
LBBB = Left Axis Deviation:
LBBB is typically associated with a normal axis or Left Axis Deviation. The presence
of Right Axis Deviation in the context of an LBBB pattern is highly atypical and
should prompt a search for alternative diagnoses (e.g., severe RVH masking LBBB,
or electrode misplacement).
RBBB + RAD = Bifascicular Block:
A simple RBBB usually has a normal axis. The combination of RBBB and RAD suggests a more extensive conduction system problem, such as a bifascicular block
(RBBB + Left Posterior Fascicular Block).
The Hemiblocks:
Left Anterior Fascicular Block (LAFB) is the most common cause of LAD. Left
Posterior Fascicular Block (LPFB) is a rare cause of RAD.
S1Q3T3 Pattern in PE:
While the classic S1Q3T3 pattern (deep S in I, Q in III, inverted T in III) is associated with PE and RAD, it is relatively insensitive. New onset RAD or RBBB in the
context of hypoxia is more clinically significant for acute right heart strain.
Normal Variant:
RAD can be a normal finding in children and tall, thin adults. LAD can be a normal
finding in obese individuals.
Lateral MI Vector Shift:

Myocardial infarction shifts the QRS axis away from the infarcted zone. A lateral
MI (involving leads I and aVL) results in a loss of R-wave voltage in those leads,
shifting the mean electrical axis to the right (RAD).
Diagnosing LPFB:
Left Posterior Fascicular Block is a diagnosis of exclusion. It causes RAD, but you
must first rule out Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH) and lateral MI, which are
more common causes of rightward axis shift.
ASD Axis Discrimination:
The axis helps distinguish Atrial Septal Defect types. Ostium secundum ASD typically presents with Right Axis Deviation and RBBB. In contrast, Ostium primum
ASD (part of AVSD) classically presents with Left Axis Deviation and RBBB.
Pulmonary Disease Effect:
Chronic lung disease (COPD, emphysema) causes hyperinflation, leading to a vertical heart position and a rightward axis shift, often accompanied by poor R-wave
progression and low voltage.
Toxicity Signs:
Sodium channel blocker toxicity (e.g., tricyclic antidepressants) causes a rightward
axis shift of the terminal 40ms of the QRS. This manifests as a dominant R-wave in
lead aVR (R wave > 3mm).
Lead Reversal Mimic:
Reversal of the Right Arm and Left Arm electrodes creates a pseudo-Right Axis
Deviation and inverted P-waves in lead I (global negativity in lead I), mimicking
dextrocardia.
WPW Mimicry:
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome can mimic axis deviations and hypertrophy. A left
lateral accessory pathway produces a dominant R wave in V1 (mimicking RVH) and
Right Axis Deviation.

question:
A 55-year-old male patient presents to the ICU with persistent low-grade fever,
pleuritic chest pain, and a pericardial friction rub, four weeks after a myocardial
infarction. His ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. What is the most likely
diagnosis?

options.text: Early post-infarction pericarditis
Dressler's syndrome
Acute pericardial tamponade
Recurrent acute coronary syndrome

Acute myocarditis

Correct answerDressler's syndrome

correctAnswer: Dressler's syndrome
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
The timing of the presentation is the key feature that distinguishes Dressler's syndrome from other forms of post-MI pericarditis.
Pathophysiology:
Dressler's syndrome is a form of late post-myocardial infarction pericarditis.
It is believed to be an autoimmune phenomenon. The initial myocardial infarction causes necrosis and the release of cardiac antigens into the bloodstream. In
susceptible individuals, this triggers an autoimmune response where the body forms
antibodies against these cardiac antigens. Weeks later, these antibodies can attack
the pericardium, pleura, and lungs, causing a delayed inflammatory response (pericarditis, pleuritis, pneumonitis).
Clinical Features and Timing:
The classic presentation is a triad of fever, pleuritic chest pain, and a pericardial
friction rub. It typically occurs 2 to 6 weeks (sometimes months) after the initial
MI. This contrasts with early post-infarction pericarditis (A), which is a direct
inflammatory reaction to adjacent myocardial necrosis occurring within the first
few days (typically days 1-3) post-MI. The presentation at four weeks fits the timeline for Dressler's syndrome (Post-Cardiac Injury Syndrome).
Diagnostic Criteria:
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR), ECG changes
(diffuse ST elevation, PR depression), and echocardiography (to assess for pericardial effusion). It falls under the umbrella of Post-Cardiac Injury Syndromes (PCIS).
Clinical Pearl
Early vs. Late:
The key differentiator is timing. Early post-infarction pericarditis occurs within
days (usually <1 week). Dressler's syndrome occurs weeks to months later.
Autoimmune Basis:
Think of Dressler's as an autoimmune, delayed hypersensitivity reaction to the
patient's own heart muscle antigens released during the MI.
Treatment Strategy:
High-dose Aspirin (e.g., 750-1000 mg) is the preferred first-line anti-inflammatory
in post-MI patients. Other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) are generally avoided as they
may interfere with myocardial healing or the antiplatelet effect of low-dose aspirin.
Colchicine is added to reduce recurrence rates.

Incidence:
Dressler's syndrome has become much less common in the era of reperfusion therapy (PCI), as rapidly restoring blood flow limits the extent of myocardial necrosis
and antigen release.
Post-Cardiac Injury Syndrome:
The same autoimmune phenomenon can occur after other forms of cardiac injury,
such as cardiac surgery or trauma, where it is known more broadly as 'post-cardiac
injury syndrome.'
ECG Specifics:
While diffuse ST elevation is classic, look specifically for PR segment depression
(except in aVR where it is elevated). This is highly specific for acute pericarditis.
Effusion Surveillance:
Echocardiography is mandatory in suspected Dressler's syndrome to quantify pericardial effusion and rule out tamponade, even if haemodynamics are currently
stable.
Anticoagulation Risks:
Therapeutic anticoagulation should be reviewed and often suspended in significant
pericarditis due to the risk of haemorrhagic transformation of the pericardial fluid,
which can rapidly lead to tamponade.
Corticosteroid Caution:
Corticosteroids are second-line agents and should be avoided if possible. They are
associated with a higher risk of recurrent pericarditis and may impair myocardial
scar formation in the post-MI setting.
ECG Morphology:
Distinguish pericarditis from STEMI by the shape of the ST elevation: pericarditis
typically shows concave upwards ('saddle-shaped') elevation, whereas STEMI shows
convex upwards ('tombstone') elevation.
Spodick's Sign:
A subtle but specific ECG sign of acute pericarditis is Spodick's sign: a downsloping
TP segment. This is best visualised in lead II and lateral precordial leads.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding mechanical ventilation for severe
asthma is NOT true?

options.text:
The goal is to minimize dynamic hyperinflation by using a low respiratory rate
and long expiratory time.
Permissive hypercapnia is often adopted to avoid barotrauma.
High levels of PEEP are used to maintain alveolar recruitment.

Disconnecting the ventilator circuit for manual decompression may be
necessary.

Volume-controlled ventilation is a commonly used mode.

Correct answerHigh levels of PEEP are used to maintain alveolar recruitment.

correctAnswer: High levels of PEEP are used to maintain alveolar recruitment.
englishExplanation:
Analysis of the False Statement:
Option C is the false statement. In severe asthma, the primary pathology is airway
resistance and air trapping, not alveolar collapse. Applying high levels of extrinsic
PEEP (ePEEP) does not recruit alveoli but instead increases intrathoracic pressure,
worsens dynamic hyperinflation, and precipitates cardiovascular collapse. While
low levels of ePEEP (<5 cmH₂O) are occasionally debated to match intrinsic PEEP
(iPEEP) in spontaneously breathing patients to reduce triggering work, high levels
for recruitment are contraindicated.
Pathophysiology of Dynamic Hyperinflation:
The profound bronchospasm in severe asthma massively increases airway resistance. This prolongs the expiratory time constant (Time Constant = Resistance x
Compliance). For complete exhalation, approximately 3 to 4 time constants are required. When the expiratory time (Te) is insufficient for the lungs to return to functional residual capacity (FRC) before the next breath starts, gas is trapped. This
leads to intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP), dynamic hyperinflation, and increased intrathoracic pressure, which impairs venous return and can cause obstructive shock.
Ventilation Strategy:
The strategy focuses on minimizing air trapping (auto-PEEP) and preventing barotrauma:
* Low Respiratory Rate and Long Expiratory Time (Option A): This is the
cornerstone of management. Rates of 6–10 breaths/min maximize expiratory time
(Te) to allow lung emptying.
* Permissive Hypercapnia (Option B): Achieving normocapnia is often impossible without causing dangerous air trapping. Hypercapnia (pH >7.15–7.20) is tolerated to prioritize safe plateau pressures.
* Manual Decompression (Option D): If severe hypotension or cardiac arrest
occurs, the patient should be disconnected from the ventilator. Manual compression
of the chest helps expel trapped gas and reduce intrathoracic pressure to restore venous return.
* Mode Selection (Option E): Volume-controlled ventilation (VCV) is commonly
used because it guarantees tidal volume delivery despite varying airway resistance
and allows precise control of inspiratory flow (square wave) to minimize inspiratory
time.

Clinical Pearl
The Enemy is Auto-PEEP:
The primary goal of ventilating an asthmatic is to allow as much time as possible for
exhalation to prevent the build-up of auto-PEEP.
'Low and Slow':
Adopt a 'Low and Slow' strategy: Low respiratory rate (6–10 bpm) and moderate
tidal volumes (6–8 ml/kg PBW). The minute volume is deliberately reduced to extend expiratory time (I:E ratio 1:4 or 1:5).
High Inspiratory Flow:
Set a high inspiratory flow rate (60–80 L/min) or a short inspiratory time (Ti
<1.0s). This delivers the breath quickly, leaving maximum time in the cycle for
exhalation.
Monitor Plateau and Auto-PEEP:
Distinguish Peak vs. Plateau pressures. In asthma, Peak Inspiratory Pressure (PIP)
is often very high due to airway resistance and is not a marker of alveolar distension. Plateau pressure (Pplat) reflects alveolar pressure; keep Pplat <30 cmH₂O to
avoid barotrauma.
Manual Decompression:
If the patient becomes acutely hypotensive or difficult to ventilate, immediately disconnect them from the ventilator. Apply manual compression to the chest wall (bear
hug) to facilitate expiration of trapped gas. This reduces intrathoracic pressure and
restores venous return.
Neuromuscular Blockade:
Early neuromuscular blockade is often required in intubated asthmatics to eliminate patient-ventilator dyssynchrony, abolish expiratory muscle activity, and facilitate permissive hypercapnia.
Troubleshooting Hypotension:
Hypotension in a ventilated asthmatic is tension pneumothorax or dynamic hyperinflation until proven otherwise. Disconnect the circuit, allow exhalation (apnoea),
and administer fluids while assessing for pneumothorax.
Time Constant Physiology:
The time constant (tau) is the product of Resistance and Compliance. In asthma,
high resistance creates a very long time constant. Since complete emptying requires
3-4 time constants, a standard expiratory time is insufficient, necessitating the 'low
and slow' strategy.
Ketamine as Induction Agent:

Ketamine is the induction agent of choice for intubating severe asthmatics. It provides bronchodilation via NMDA receptor antagonism and interference with calcium handling in smooth muscle, alongside maintaining sympathetic tone.
Magnesium Sulphate Role:
Intravenous magnesium sulphate (1.2-2g) acts as a smooth muscle relaxant by
blocking calcium channels. It is a standard adjunct in severe asthma unresponsive
to beta-agonists and steroids.
Extrinsic PEEP (ZEEP):
In controlled ventilation for asthma, extrinsic PEEP is typically set to zero (ZEEP).
Unlike COPD, where low PEEP may splint open dynamic airway collapse (waterfall
effect), in asthma, extrinsic PEEP often simply adds to the total intrathoracic pressure, worsening hyperinflation.
Permissive Hypercapnia Limits:
Hypercapnia is generally well tolerated, but pH <7.15 may require buffering with bicarbonate or THAM to ensure catecholamine responsiveness. Contraindications to
permissive hypercapnia include raised intracranial pressure and severe pulmonary
hypertension.

question:
A patient on long-term amiodarone therapy develops thyrotoxicosis. A diagnosis
of Type II amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) is suspected. Which finding
would be most consistent with this diagnosis?

options.text: A very high radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) value.
A very low or near-absent radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) value.
The presence of TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb).
Markedly increased vascularity on thyroid color-flow Doppler ultrasound.

A slow, indolent clinical course.

Correct answerA very low or near-absent radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) value.

correctAnswer: A very low or near-absent radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) value.
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology:
The key to differentiating the two types of AIT is determining if the gland is overproducing hormone (Type I) or leaking pre-formed hormone (Type II). Type II AIT
is a destructive thyroiditis caused by a direct toxic effect of amiodarone. The gland is
inflamed and destroyed, releasing pre-formed hormone, but it is not synthesizing
new hormone.
Diagnostic Investigations:
Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) is a critical discriminator. In Type II AIT (destructive thyroiditis), the gland is damaged and leaks pre-formed hormone without
synthesizing new hormone; consequently, RAIU is typically <1%
(absent/suppressed). In Type I AIT, despite the massive iodine load from amiodarone which usually suppresses uptake, the autonomous hyperfunctioning tissue
maintains detectable or even normal/high uptake.
Vascularity (Doppler):
Thyroid ultrasound with colour flow Doppler is the other key investigation. Type I
AIT typically shows increased vascularity ('thyroid inferno'), whereas Type II AIT
shows absent or reduced vascularity due to follicular destruction.
Clinical Pearl
Pathophysiological Distinction:
Type I AIT involves hyper-synthesis of hormone (Jod-Basedow effect), whereas
Type II involves the destructive release of pre-formed hormone (thyroiditis).
RAIU Differentiates:
In the context of amiodarone loading, 'normal' or 'detectable' RAIU strongly suggests Type I, as the massive iodine pool should physiologically suppress uptake to
zero. Type II is characterized by absent (<1%) uptake.
Doppler Ultrasound Findings:
Increased blood flow (hypervascularity) on Doppler suggests the hyperactive gland
of Type I. Absent or low blood flow suggests the destructive process of Type II.
Targeted Management Strategies:
Type I is treated with antithyroid drugs (carbimazole) to block synthesis; potassium
perchlorate may be added to discharge iodine. Type II is treated with high-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone) to reduce inflammation.
Spectrum of Thyroid Dysfunction:

Amiodarone can cause both hypothyroidism (more common) and hyperthyroidism
due to its high iodine content and direct cellular toxicity.
Mixed AIT Presentation:
Differentiation is not always binary. Many patients exhibit 'Mixed AIT' with features
of both types. Guidelines recommend starting both carbimazole and prednisolone if
the diagnosis is indeterminate, then tapering based on response.
Pharmacokinetic Considerations:
Amiodarone is 37% iodine by weight and has a half-life of up to 100 days. Stopping
the drug does not resolve thyrotoxicosis acutely and may exacerbate Type I AIT by
removing the Wolff-Chaikoff inhibitory effect while leaving the iodine substrate.
Interleukin-6 as Discriminator:
Serum Interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels are often markedly elevated in Type II AIT due to
the destructive inflammatory process, whereas they typically remain normal or only
slightly elevated in Type I AIT.
Sestamibi Scintigraphy:
99mTc-Sestamibi scanning can aid diagnosis when RAIU is indeterminate. Type I
AIT typically shows persistent uptake, while Type II AIT shows rapid washout or absent uptake.
Iodine Load Magnitude:
A single 200 mg tablet of amiodarone contains approximately 75 mg of organic iodine. Metabolism releases about 7 mg of free iodine daily, which is roughly 50 times
the recommended daily iodine intake (0.15 mg).
Long-term Sequelae:
Type II AIT often progresses to permanent hypothyroidism. The destructive process
eventually leads to fibrosis and follicular atrophy, unlike Type I where thyroid function may return to baseline after treatment.

question:
A 30-year-old woman with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) presents with
high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Laboratory tests show a ferritin of 8,000 µg/L. You suspect Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS).
Which of the following laboratory findings is most specific for the T-cell activation seen in HLH/MAS?

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate showing evidence of hemophagocytosis.
Elevated serum ferritin levels above 5,000 µg/L.
Elevated soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) levels.
Hypertriglyceridemia and hypofibrinogenemia.

Elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT) and LDH.

Correct answerElevated soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) levels.

correctAnswer: Elevated soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) levels.
englishExplanation:
Diagnosis:
The question is assessing understanding of laboratory findings that are indicative of
Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS), a condition associated with
Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). The correct answer is elevated soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) levels, which indicates T-cell activation.
Pathophysiology:
Macrophage Activation Syndrome is a severe, potentially life-threatening condition
characterized by excessive activation and proliferation of macrophages and T-cells.
In MAS, there is a dysregulation of immune responses leading to excessive cytokine
release, also known as a "cytokine storm." T-cells, when activated, express the alpha
chain of the IL-2 receptor, known as CD25. Soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) reflects the level
of T-cell activation in the body because its levels increase when it is shed from activated T-cells into the bloodstream.
Why C is Correct:
Elevated soluble CD25 (sIL-2R) levels are specifically associated with T-cell activation, making it a critical marker in the context of HLH/MAS. In this case, the
patient's clinical presentation including high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia, along with elevated ferritin, suggests MAS, hence measuring sIL-2R levels
helps in confirming significant T-cell activation characteristic of HLH/MAS.
Key Distinguishing Feature:
While several laboratory findings may indicate MAS or support a diagnosis of HLH,
elevated sIL-2R is directly linked to T-cell activation, which is a core feature of the
syndrome. This marker not only assists in diagnosis but also correlates with disease
activity, making it distinct from other laboratory parameters that may reflect secondary changes or other complications.
Why Not the Others:
A: Bone marrow aspirate showing evidence of hemophagocytosis is important for
diagnosis but is not specific for T-cell activation; it can also occur in a variety of
other conditions.
B: Elevated serum ferritin levels above 5,000 µg/L, though suggestive, is not specific for T-cell activation as high ferritin can occur in several inflammatory conditions.

D: Hypertriglyceridemia and hypofibrinogenemia are indicative of systemic inflammation and liver involvement but do not specifically indicate T-cell activation.
E: Elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT) and LDH are reflective of systemic inflammation and organ dysfunction and are not specific to T-cell activation.
Clinical Pearl
HLH Pathophysiology:
HLH is characterised by uncontrolled immune activation with macrophage and cytotoxic T-cell hyperactivity, leading to a cytokine storm.
sCD25 Significance:
sCD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor alpha-chain) is shed by activated T-cells and directly
reflects the degree of pathological T-cell activation in HLH.
Ferritin Threshold:
Ferritin >10,000 mcg/L is strongly suggestive of HLH but not pathognomonic - it
can also rise in sepsis, liver failure, and other inflammatory states.
HLH-2004 Criteria:
Diagnosis requires 5 of 8 features: fever, splenomegaly, 2+ cytopenias,
hypertriglyceridaemia/hypofibrinogenaemia, haemophagocytosis, low NK activity,
sCD25 >=2400 U/mL, ferritin >=500 mcg/L.
Hypertriglyceridaemia Mechanism:
Cytokines (particularly TNF-alpha and IL-1) inhibit lipoprotein lipase activity, causing hypertriglyceridaemia.
Hypofibrinogenaemia:
Hypofibrinogenaemia reflects consumptive coagulopathy driven by macrophage activation and DIC - a marker of disease severity.
Haemophagocytosis Caveat:
Bone marrow haemophagocytosis lacks specificity (also seen in sepsis) and may be
absent early in HLH - it is not required for diagnosis.
Secondary HLH Triggers:
Secondary HLH most commonly occurs in SLE, lymphoma, EBV infection, and sepsis - always identify and treat the underlying trigger.
The H-Score:
The H-Score is a validated clinical tool used to estimate the probability of reactive
haemophagocytic syndrome (secondary HLH/MAS). It incorporates nine parameters: temperature, organomegaly (hepatomegaly, splenomegaly), number of cytopenias, triglycerides, fibrinogen, ferritin, AST, immunosuppressed status, and evidence of haemophagocytosis on bone marrow aspirate. Scores are weighted and

summed - a score >169 carries >93% probability of HLH. Unlike the HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria, the H-Score was specifically developed and validated for
secondary/reactive HLH in adults and is increasingly used as the primary bedside
diagnostic tool in ICU practice. An online calculator is freely available at
mdcalc.com.

question:
A 45-year-old farmer presents with agitation, copious oral secretions, pinpoint
pupils, vomiting, and diarrhea after working with insecticides. Which of the following is NOT an appropriate management step?

options.text: Administer high-dose atropine to control muscarinic symptoms.
Administer pralidoxime (an oxime) to reactivate acetylcholinesterase.
Administer benzodiazepines for seizures or severe agitation.
Initiate haemodialysis for enhanced elimination of the toxin.

Remove all contaminated clothing and wash the skin thoroughly.

Correct answerInitiate haemodialysis for enhanced elimination of the toxin.

correctAnswer: Initiate haemodialysis for enhanced elimination of the toxin.
englishExplanation:
Analysis of the Correct Answer:
Haemodialysis is NOT indicated in organophosphate (OP) poisoning. OPs are
highly lipid-soluble and have a large volume of distribution (Vd), meaning they are
sequestered in tissues and not accessible in the plasma for extracorporeal removal.
While haemoperfusion has been theoretically suggested, it is not standard care.
Management focuses on decontamination and antidotal therapy.
Standard Management (TOXBASE Guidelines):
1. Decontamination: Immediate removal of clothing and irrigation of skin. Staff
must wear appropriate PPE to prevent secondary poisoning (cutaneous absorption).
2. Resuscitation: Airway protection is critical due to bronchorrhoea and respiratory muscle weakness.
3. Atropine: The mainstay of therapy for muscarinic effects (bronchorrhoea,
bradycardia). It acts as a competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Doses are doubled every 5-10 minutes until the endpoint (drying of secretions)
is reached.
4. Oximes (Pralidoxime): Reactivate acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphate group from the enzyme's active site. This is crucial for treating nicotinic effects (neuromuscular weakness) which atropine does not address. Most effective if
given early before enzyme 'aging' occurs.
5. Benzodiazepines: Administered for seizures and agitation; they also reduce
central respiratory depression and neurotoxicity.
Mechanism of Toxicity:
Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase (AChE) by
phosphorylating the serine hydroxyl group at the esteratic site. This leads to the accumulation of acetylcholine at both muscarinic receptors (causing DUMBBELS
symptoms) and nicotinic receptors (causing fasciculations and neuromuscular
paralysis).
Clinical Pearl
Cholinergic Toxidrome Presentation:
Recall the Cholinergic Toxidrome: DUMBBELS (Diarrhoea, Urination, Miosis,
Bradycardia, Bronchorrhoea, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation) or SLUDGE.
Bronchorrhoea is the primary cause of mortality due to airway obstruction and
hypoxia.
Atropine Mechanism and Endpoint:

Atropine reverses muscarinic effects (secretions, bradycardia) but has NO effect on
nicotinic symptoms (muscle weakness/paralysis). The therapeutic endpoint is clear
lungs (drying of secretions), NOT heart rate or pupil size. Tachycardia is not a contraindication to further doses if secretions persist.
Role of Oximes:
Pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase by displacing the organophosphate
from the enzyme's active site. It is specifically indicated to treat nicotinic effects
(neuromuscular weakness, fasciculations, diaphragmatic paralysis) because atropine has no effect on the neuromuscular junction.
Secondary Contamination Risk:
Organophosphates are readily absorbed through the skin. Healthcare staff must
wear appropriate PPE (gloves, aprons, eye protection) during decontamination to
avoid secondary poisoning from contact with the patient's skin, clothing, or vomit.
Enzyme Aging Mechanism:
Organophosphates bind to acetylcholinesterase initially in a reversible manner.
Over time (minutes to hours), the phosphate group undergoes a chemical change
(loss of an alkyl group) known as 'aging', rendering the enzyme-inhibitor complex
permanent. Once aging occurs, oximes are ineffective, and new enzyme synthesis is
required.
Intermediate Syndrome:
A distinct clinical entity occurring 24-96 hours after exposure, characterized by
proximal muscle weakness (neck flexion, cranial nerves, respiratory muscles) often
requiring re-intubation. It is distinct from the acute cholinergic crisis and delayed
neuropathy.
Atropinisation Protocol:
Use a doubling dose strategy (e.g., 2mg, 4mg, 8mg) every 5-10 minutes. Massive cumulative doses (hundreds of mg) may be required in severe poisoning. The goal is
drying of bronchial secretions.
Carbamate vs Organophosphate Poisoning:
Carbamates also inhibit acetylcholinesterase but the bond is transient (carbamylation) and spontaneously hydrolyses within hours. 'Aging' does not occur, the duration of toxicity is shorter, and oximes are generally not indicated.
Biomarkers of Exposure:
Red blood cell (RBC) acetylcholinesterase activity is the preferred biomarker as it
correlates well with synaptic enzyme function. Plasma butyrylcholinesterase is more
easily assayed but is less specific and levels may be depressed by other conditions
(e.g., liver disease, pregnancy).

question:
A patient on long-term amiodarone for atrial fibrillation is being counseled on
the drug's properties. Which statement accurately describes the pharmacokinetics of amiodarone?

options.text:
Amiodarone has a very short half-life of 2-3 hours and is primarily cleared by the
kidneys.

Amiodarone is a prodrug that must be activated by the liver to its active form,
desethylamiodarone.

Due to its high water solubility, amiodarone is rapidly eliminated and has few
drug interactions.

Amiodarone is highly lipophilic, extensively distributed into tissues, and has an
extremely long elimination half-life.
Dose adjustments for amiodarone are primarily based on renal function.

correctAnswer:
Amiodarone is highly lipophilic, extensively distributed into tissues, and has an
extremely long elimination half-life.
englishExplanation:
Pharmacokinetics:
Amiodarone is highly lipophilic and has a massive volume of distribution (approx.
66 L/kg). It distributes extensively into adipose tissue and highly perfused organs
(liver, lungs, spleen), acting as a deep tissue reservoir.
Metabolism and Excretion:
Metabolism is primarily hepatic via CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 to the active metabolite
desethylamiodarone. Elimination is biphasic with a terminal half-life ranging from
20 to 100 days due to slow release from tissue stores. Excretion is almost exclusively
biliary/faecal; renal clearance is negligible, rendering dose adjustment in renal failure unnecessary.
Clinical Pearl
Loading Dose is Required:
Because of its huge volume of distribution, a large oral or IV loading dose is required to quickly saturate the tissue compartments and achieve a therapeutic
plasma concentration.
Long Half-Life, Long Memory:
The extremely long half-life means that side effects and drug interactions can persist for weeks or months after the drug is stopped.
The "Big 3" Interactions:
Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9, P-glycoprotein, and CYP3A4. This necessitates dose
reductions for Warfarin (inhibits metabolism, rising INR), Digoxin (inhibits P-gp
efflux, rising levels), and Simvastatin (inhibits metabolism, risk of rhabdomyolysis).
The "Big 6" Monitoring Parameters:
UK monitoring guidelines (NICE CKS) mandate: Baseline CXR, ECG, TFTs, LFTs,
and Potassium. Maintenance requires TFTs and LFTs every 6 months. Routine ophthalmology and respiratory testing is symptom-driven, though a low threshold for
investigation is required.
Iodine Content:
Amiodarone contains a large amount of iodine, which is the primary reason for its
complex effects on the thyroid gland (causing both hypothyroidism and
hyperthyroidism).
Vaughan Williams Classification:

Although classified as a Class III antiarrhythmic (potassium channel blocker), amiodarone possesses properties of all four classes: sodium channel blockade (Class I),
beta-blockade (Class II), and calcium channel blockade (Class IV).
IV Administration Risks:
Intravenous amiodarone is highly phlebitic. It should ideally be administered via a
central venous catheter (CVC). If peripheral administration is unavoidable, use a
large vein and concentrations <2 mg/mL to reduce risk of thrombophlebitis.
Blue-Grey Skin Discoloration:
Chronic accumulation of amiodarone and lipofuscin in the dermis can lead to a
characteristic slate-grey or blue skin discoloration in sun-exposed areas (pseudocyanosis), which may persist for months after cessation.
Pulmonary Toxicity Mechanism:
Amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity (AIPT) occurs via direct cytotoxic effects
and phospholipidosis (accumulation of phospholipid-laden macrophages). It typically presents as a non-productive cough and dyspnoea, with CXR showing diffuse
interstitial infiltrates. The risk increases with cumulative dose and high FiO2.
Thyroid Dysfunction Types:
Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) has two forms: Type 1 occurs in abnormal
thyroids (e.g., multinodular goitre) via the Jod-Basedow effect (iodine-induced excess synthesis). Type 2 occurs in normal thyroids via destructive thyroiditis (release
of pre-formed hormone). Type 2 is often treated with corticosteroids.
Corneal Microdeposits:
Corneal microdeposits occur in nearly all patients on long-term therapy. They result
from the secretion of amiodarone by the lacrimal gland and subsequent corneal uptake. While they can cause halos around lights, they rarely affect visual acuity and
are not an indication to stop therapy unless vision is impaired.
Acute Haemodynamic Effects:
Rapid IV administration can cause hypotension and bradycardia. This is partly due
to the negative inotropic and chronotropic effects of the drug itself, but also due to
solvents (e.g., polysorbate 80 or benzyl alcohol) in certain formulations, which
cause histamine release and direct vasodilation.

question:
A 55-year-old male presents with a sudden, severe headache. A CT scan confirms
an acute intracerebral haemorrhage. His admission blood pressure is 210/115
mmHg. What is the current guideline-recommended target for systolic blood
pressure in the acute phase?

options.text: Rapidly lower systolic BP to a target of 140 mmHg
Maintain systolic BP above 180 mmHg to ensure cerebral perfusion
Lower mean arterial pressure by no more than 15%
Start an oral antihypertensive for gradual reduction over 48 hours

Withhold treatment unless BP exceeds 220 mmHg

Correct answerRapidly lower systolic BP to a target of 140 mmHg

correctAnswer: Rapidly lower systolic BP to a target of 140 mmHg
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
The management of blood pressure in acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH) is different from that of ischaemic stroke and focuses on limiting the
extent of the bleed.
Pathophysiology:
An ICH occurs when a small artery within the brain parenchyma ruptures, often due
to chronic damage from hypertension. Active bleeding can continue for several
hours after the initial rupture, leading to an expansion of the haematoma. This
haematoma expansion is a major cause of neurological deterioration and poor outcomes, as it increases intracranial pressure (ICP) and causes direct mechanical
damage to surrounding brain tissue. High systemic blood pressure is thought to
contribute directly to this continued bleeding and haematoma expansion.
Management Rationale:
The primary goal of acute BP management in ICH is to reduce the hydrostatic pressure driving the bleeding, thereby limiting haematoma expansion without compromising cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP). NICE NG128 recommends offering rapid
blood pressure lowering to people with acute spontaneous ICH who present within
6 hours of symptom onset and have a systolic BP between 150 and 220 mmHg. The
specific target is a systolic blood pressure of 130 to 140 mmHg, to be achieved
within 1 hour of starting treatment. While the INTERACT2 trial suggested benefit
from intensive lowering, the ATACH-2 trial highlighted risks of renal injury with
overly aggressive targets (<120 mmHg), solidifying the 130-140 mmHg consensus
range.
Physiological Considerations:
Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) is defined as Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) minus Intracranial Pressure (ICP). In patients with significant mass effect and raised
ICP, lowering systemic blood pressure risks reducing CPP below the critical threshold for ischaemia (typically <60-70 mmHg). However, evidence suggests that in the
absence of large haematomas causing herniation syndromes, the benefit of limiting
haematoma expansion via BP control outweighs the theoretical risk of ischaemia in
the peri-haematoma region.
Clinical Pearl
Haematoma Expansion Risk:

The greatest risk of haematoma expansion occurs within the first few hours of an
ICH. Therefore, blood pressure control should be initiated as soon as possible after
diagnosis to mitigate this risk.
Differential Management Targets:
Differentiation is critical. In ICH, BP is lowered aggressively to a target SBP of 130140 mmHg to limit haematoma expansion. In ischaemic stroke (without thrombolysis), permissive hypertension is generally allowed (up to 220/120 mmHg) to maintain collateral perfusion to the ischaemic penumbra.
Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP):
While lowering BP, one must be mindful of maintaining adequate CPP, which is calculated as MAP - ICP. In patients with very large haematomas and high ICP, the BP
target may need to be adjusted upwards to maintain a CPP > 60 mmHg.
Antihypertensive Selection:
Intravenous agents with short half-lives are preferred for precise titration. IV labetalol (combined alpha-1 and non-selective beta-blocker) is a standard first-line
agent. GTN is often avoided as a primary agent because it is a nitric oxide donor
causing cerebral venodilation, which increases cerebral blood volume and potentially raises ICP.
Risks of Aggressive Lowering:
Avoid hypotension (SBP <120-130 mmHg). The ATACH-2 trial demonstrated that
very intensive lowering increased the rate of renal adverse events without improving
neurological outcomes compared to the standard 140 mmHg target.
Target Achievement Window:
NICE NG128 explicitly recommends achieving the target systolic blood pressure of
130-140 mmHg within 1 hour of starting treatment to maximise efficacy in preventing haematoma expansion.
Maintenance Duration:
Once the target blood pressure (130-140 mmHg) is achieved, it should be maintained for at least 7 days to prevent re-bleeding and stabilise the haematoma.
Cushing's Reflex Awareness:
Be cautious in patients presenting with the Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration). This indicates significantly raised ICP with impending
herniation. In this specific context, the hypertension is a compensatory mechanism
to maintain cerebral perfusion; aggressive lowering before ICP management may
precipitate ischaemia or death.
Cerebral Autoregulation Shift:

Chronic hypertension causes a rightward shift in the cerebral autoregulation curve.
These patients require higher mean arterial pressures to maintain cerebral blood
flow compared to normotensive individuals, making them more susceptible to ischaemia if blood pressure is normalised too rapidly or aggressively.
Anticoagulation Reversal:
Blood pressure control must be parallel to immediate reversal of coagulopathy.
Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is indicated for warfarin-associated ICH.
Specific reversal agents (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for
apixaban/rivaroxaban) should be used for DOAC-associated haemorrhage where
available.
Surgical Indications:
The STICH and STICH II trials generally showed no benefit for early surgery over
conservative management for deep supratentorial haemorrhages. Surgery is typically reserved for superficial lobar haemorrhages with mass effect, or cerebellar
haemorrhages (>3 cm) causing hydrocephalus or brainstem compression.

question:
Which of the following is the primary mechanism by which lithium causes
hypothyroidism?

options.text: It destroys thyroid follicular cells via an autoimmune reaction.
It increases the peripheral conversion of T₄ to T₃.

It inhibits multiple steps in thyroid hormone synthesis and blocks the release of
T₄ and T₃ from the gland.
It acts as a TSH receptor agonist, causing downregulation of the receptors.
It accelerates the renal clearance of thyroid hormones.

correctAnswer:
It inhibits multiple steps in thyroid hormone synthesis and blocks the release of
T₄ and T₃ from the gland.
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Lithium accumulates in the thyroid gland at concentrations 3-4 times higher than
plasma. Its primary mechanism of inducing hypothyroidism is the inhibition of thyroid hormone release from the gland (inhibiting colloid pinocytosis). It also inhibits
thyroid hormone synthesis (via thyroid peroxidase inhibition) and decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 (inhibiting type I 5'-deiodinase). The resulting decrease in circulating T4/T3 stimulates TSH secretion, leading to goitre and potentially overt hypothyroidism.
Clinical Pearl
Lithium Blocks Synthesis and Release:
This dual-action is its main effect on the thyroid.
Goitre and Hypothyroidism:
These are the most frequent thyroid-related side effects of long-term lithium
therapy.
Monitor TFTs Regularly:
NICE guidelines mandate checking thyroid function (TSH, free T4) at baseline and
every 6 months during maintenance treatment.
Treatment is Levothyroxine:
If a patient on lithium develops hypothyroidism, the treatment is to add levothyroxine; it is not usually necessary to stop the lithium.
Other Endocrine Effects:
Lithium can also cause hyperparathyroidism (leading to hypercalcaemia) and
nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus Mechanism:
Lithium enters principal cells of the collecting duct via ENaC channels and interferes with aquaporin-2 expression, causing ADH resistance. This is managed with
amiloride (blocks ENaC) rather than fluid restriction.
Drug Interactions Increasing Toxicity:
Renal clearance of lithium is reduced by ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, and thiazide diuretics. Concurrent use requires careful monitoring to prevent toxicity.
Therapeutic Index:
Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window (0.4–1.0 mmol/L). Toxicity signs include
coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, and seizures; levels >1.5 mmol/L require urgent

assessment.
Renal Handling and Sodium:
Lithium is handled similarly to sodium in the proximal tubule. Any condition causing hyponatraemia or dehydration leads to compensatory sodium retention, which
simultaneously increases lithium reabsorption and precipitates toxicity.
Severe Toxicity Management:
Haemodialysis is indicated for severe toxicity (levels >4.0 mmol/L, or >2.5 mmol/L
with significant neurological symptoms or renal failure) as lithium is a small molecule with a low volume of distribution.
Cardiovascular Side Effects:
Lithium can cause benign T-wave inversion, sinus node dysfunction, and rarely
arrhythmias.
Teratogenicity Risk:
Lithium use in the first trimester is associated with Ebstein's anomaly (tricuspid
valve defect), though the absolute risk is lower than historically reported.

question:
A 50-year-old woman with diffuse systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) who was recently started on high-dose prednisone for her skin disease presents with the
abrupt onset of a blood pressure of 220/130 mmHg and acute oliguric renal failure. Her peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. What is the specific, life-saving treatment for this condition?

options.text: Immediate plasma exchange.
An infusion of a potent vasodilator like sodium nitroprusside.
High-dose intravenous corticosteroids.
An ACE inhibitor, titrated to normalize blood pressure.

Emergent haemodialysis.

Correct answerAn ACE inhibitor, titrated to normalize blood pressure.

correctAnswer: An ACE inhibitor, titrated to normalize blood pressure.
englishExplanation:
Pathophysiology and Diagnosis:
Scleroderma Renal Crisis (SRC) is a medical emergency characterised by malignant
hypertension and acute kidney injury, occurring in 5-10% of systemic sclerosis patients. The pathology is often described as 'renal Raynaud's phenomenon', where severe renal vasospasm leads to cortical hypoperfusion and massive renin release.
This activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) drives the malignant hypertension. The presence of schistocytes indicates microangiopathic
haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), a common feature of SRC that mimics thrombotic
thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).
Management:
ACE inhibitors are the specific, life-saving treatment. They reverse the angiotensinII mediated vasoconstriction. Captopril is the preferred agent due to its short halflife, allowing rapid titration. Treatment should be initiated immediately, even in the
presence of renal failure.
Other Options:
Plasma exchange (A) is the treatment for TTP; while SRC presents with MAHA, the
underlying mechanism is RAAS-mediated rather than due to ADAMTS13 deficiency.
Corticosteroids (C) are a major precipitant of SRC and should be avoided or tapered. Haemodialysis (E) may be required for supportive care but does not treat the
underlying vasoconstriction.
Clinical Pearl
Therapeutic Cornerstone:
ACE inhibitors are the only class of drugs proven to improve survival in SRC. They
transformed SRC from a universally fatal condition to a treatable one by specifically
targeting the RAAS-driven pathophysiology.
AKI Management Exception:
Initiating ACE inhibitors in the context of acute kidney injury is typically contraindicated, but in SRC it is mandatory to break the vasoconstrictive cycle, even if
creatinine initially rises.
Risk Factors:
The main risk factors are diffuse scleroderma (as opposed to limited), the presence
of anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies, and recent corticosteroid use.
Normotensive SRC:

A small number of patients (approximately 10%) can develop the renal failure and
microangiopathy of SRC without severe hypertension. This 'normotensive SRC' carries an even worse prognosis and is frequently missed.
Captopril Titration:
Captopril is the preferred initial ACE inhibitor due to its rapid onset and short duration of action, allowing precise titration against volatile blood pressure.
Renal Recovery Potential:
Patients requiring dialysis for SRC may recover renal function up to 24 months after
onset. ACE inhibitors should be continued even during dialysis to facilitate this
recovery.
Corticosteroid Risk:
High-dose corticosteroids (typically defined as >15 mg/day of prednisone) are the
single most significant modifiable risk factor for precipitating SRC.
Prophylaxis Myth:
Prophylactic use of ACE inhibitors in systemic sclerosis patients does not prevent
SRC. Evidence suggests it may actually be harmful by masking early hypertension or
leading to worse outcomes if SRC develops.
Differential Diagnosis:
SRC can mimic Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) due to the presence
of MAHA and thrombocytopenia. However, ADAMTS13 activity is typically normal
in SRC, and the condition is driven by renin-mediated hypertension rather than primary thrombosis.
Histopathology:
Renal biopsy in SRC typically demonstrates 'onion-skin' proliferative lesions of the
interlobular arteries and arterioles, reflecting severe hypertensive injury.
Second-Line Agents:
If blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite maximal ACE inhibitor therapy, calcium channel blockers or alpha-blockers may be added. Beta-blockers should generally be avoided as they may exacerbate vasospasm via unopposed alpha-adrenergic
activity.

question:
Which of the following statements about tubes used for oesophageal variceal
tamponade is not correct?

options.text:
The Sengstaken-Blakemore tube has a gastric balloon, an oesophageal balloon,
and a gastric suction port.

The Minnesota tube is a four-lumen tube, adding an oesophageal suction port to
the Sengstaken-Blakemore design.
The Linton-Nachlas tube is a three-lumen tube similar to the SengstakenBlakemore tube.

To position a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube, the 50-55cm mark is typically aligned
with the incisors.
Inflation of the oesophageal balloon is not always required to control bleeding.

correctAnswer: The Linton-Nachlas tube is a three-lumen tube similar to the SengstakenBlakemore tube.
englishExplanation:
Answer Analysis:
Option C is the incorrect statement. While the Linton-Nachlas tube is indeed a
three-lumen tube, it is structurally and functionally distinct from the SengstakenBlakemore (SB) tube. The SB tube has two balloons (gastric and oesophageal) and
one suction port (gastric). The Linton-Nachlas tube has only one balloon (a large capacity gastric balloon) and two suction ports (gastric and oesophageal). It is specifically designed for gastric fundal varices, whereas the SB tube targets oesophageal
varices.
Physiology of Tamponade:
These tubes are designed to stop variceal bleeding by direct pressure (tamponade).
Bleeding can originate from oesophageal varices or gastric fundal varices. The design of the tube dictates which area it can effectively compress.
Tube Configurations:
1. Sengstaken-Blakemore (3 Lumens): Gastric balloon, Oesophageal balloon,
Gastric aspiration port. Lacks an oesophageal suction port, necessitating a separate
NG tube above the balloon to prevent aspiration.
2. Minnesota (4 Lumens): Gastric balloon, Oesophageal balloon, Gastric aspiration port, Oesophageal aspiration port. The addition of the oesophageal port helps
clear secretions pooling above the balloon.
3. Linton-Nachlas (3 Lumens): Large volume Gastric balloon (up to 600ml),
Gastric aspiration port, Oesophageal aspiration port. No oesophageal balloon. Used
for gastric varices.
Placement and Safety:
Insertion depth is typically 50-55cm to ensure the gastric balloon is within the
stomach. Verification via auscultation and chest x-ray is mandatory before full inflation to prevent oesophageal rupture. The oesophageal balloon (in SB/Minnesota
tubes) is only inflated if bleeding continues despite gastric balloon traction.
Clinical Pearl
Know Your Tube:
Sengstaken-Blakemore has 3 lumens (2 balloons, 1 suction). Minnesota has 4 lumens (2 balloons, 2 suction). Linton-Nachlas has 3 lumens (1 large gastric balloon,
2 suction) and is reserved for gastric varices.
Aspiration Risk:

A major risk is aspiration of secretions that pool above the inflated oesophageal balloon. The Minnesota tube was designed to mitigate this. If using a SengstakenBlakemore tube, a separate nasogastric tube should be placed in the oesophagus to
aspirate this space.
Bridge to Definitive Therapy:
Balloon tamponade is a temporary, life-saving measure ('a bridge') to control exsanguinating haemorrhage while preparing for definitive therapy (i.e., endoscopy or
TIPS procedure). It should not be left in place for more than 24 hours.
Airway Protection First:
These tubes should only be placed in a patient who has been intubated for airway
protection, due to the high risk of aspiration and airway compromise.
Oesophageal Rupture:
The most feared complication is oesophageal rupture from over-inflation of the oesophageal balloon or accidental inflation of the gastric balloon within the
oesophagus.
Verification is Vital:
Never fully inflate the gastric balloon without verifying position. Inflate with a small
volume (e.g., 50ml air), confirm position on CXR, then complete inflation.
Accidental inflation in the oesophagus causes rupture.
Sequential Deflation:
When removing the tube, always deflate the oesophageal balloon first. Deflating the
gastric balloon while the oesophageal balloon is inflated can cause the tube to migrate proximally and obstruct the airway.
Emergency Release Protocol:
A pair of scissors must be kept at the bedside at all times. If the tube migrates proximally and obstructs the airway, the lumens must be cut immediately to deflate both
balloons.
Oesophageal Balloon Pressure:
If the oesophageal balloon is inflated, pressure must be monitored and maintained
between 25-45 mmHg. Pressures exceeding this range significantly increase the risk
of oesophageal necrosis and rupture.
Gastric Balloon Volume:
The gastric balloon typically requires 250-300ml of air (check manufacturer instructions) to ensure it cannot be pulled back into the oesophagus when traction is
applied.
Traction Application:

Once the gastric balloon is inflated and position confirmed, traction (typically 1 kg)
is applied to the external portion of the tube. This pulls the balloon against the cardia, mechanically compressing the feeding vessels.

question: An LV pressure-volume loop is generated. If a patient is given a pure arterial vasodilator like sodium nitroprusside, what is the expected change in the P-V loop?

options.text: The loop shifts to the right, with an increased end-diastolic volume.
The loop becomes taller, with a higher end-systolic pressure.
The loop becomes wider, with an increased stroke volume, and the top-left corner shifts downwards and to the left along the same ESPVR.

The slope of the End-Systolic Pressure-Volume Relationship (ESPVR) becomes
steeper.
The loop becomes narrower, with a decreased stroke volume.

correctAnswer: The loop becomes wider, with an increased stroke volume, and the top-left corner shifts downwards and to the left along the same ESPVR.
englishExplanation:
