Physiology of Afterload Reduction:
A pure arterial vasodilator reduces the systemic vascular resistance (afterload)
against which the ventricle ejects. In pressure-volume loop terms, this reduces the
effective arterial elastance (Ea), which is the slope of the line connecting the end-diastolic volume to the end-systolic point. Importantly, the intrinsic contractility of
the myocardium is unchanged, so the slope of the End-Systolic Pressure-Volume
Relationship (ESPVR) line remains constant.
Impact on the P-V Loop:
Because the ventricle faces less resistance, it can shorten more effectively, resulting
in a lower End-Systolic Volume (ESV). The end-systolic point (top-left corner)
moves downwards (lower pressure) and to the left (lower volume) along the existing
ESPVR line. With a constant End-Diastolic Volume (preload), the difference between EDV and ESV increases, resulting in a wider loop and increased Stroke
Volume.
Mechanism of Action: Sodium Nitroprusside:
Sodium nitroprusside acts as a nitric oxide (NO) donor. The released NO activates
guanylate cyclase in vascular smooth muscle, increasing intracellular cGMP. This
inhibits calcium entry and promotes calcium sequestration, leading to smooth muscle relaxation. While the question models a 'pure' arterial effect, clinically SNP
causes both arterial and venous dilation.
Clinical Pearl
Afterload Reduction Visualisation:
Afterload reduction causes the end-systolic point to slide down and to the left along
the fixed ESPVR line. This results in a lower end-systolic pressure and volume.
Contractility and ESPVR Slope:
Positive inotropes increase the slope of the ESPVR (shifting it to the left), allowing
the ventricle to generate higher pressure for a given volume.
Preload and Loop Position:
An increase in preload (end-diastolic volume) shifts the right-hand vertical boundary of the loop further to the right, increasing stroke volume via the Frank-Starling
mechanism.
ESPVR as Contractility Index:

The slope of the End-Systolic Pressure-Volume Relationship (ESPVR), also known
as maximal elastance (Emax), is the most reliable index of intrinsic myocardial contractility as it is load-independent.
Stroke Work Representation:
The area contained within the P-V loop represents Stroke Work. While vasodilators
increase Stroke Volume (width), they decrease systolic pressure (height); the net effect on Stroke Work varies, but myocardial oxygen demand typically falls due to reduced wall tension.
Diastolic Compliance and EDPVR:
The bottom curve of the loop represents the End-Diastolic Pressure-Volume
Relationship (EDPVR). An upward shift of this curve indicates reduced ventricular
compliance (diastolic dysfunction), requiring higher filling pressures to achieve the
same end-diastolic volume.
Arterial Elastance (Ea):
Arterial elastance represents the afterload imposed by the vasculature. On a P-V
loop, it is depicted as the negative slope of the line connecting the end-diastolic volume on the x-axis to the end-systolic pressure-volume point. Vasodilators decrease
this slope.
Ventricular-Arterial Coupling:
Efficiency is maximised when the ratio of arterial elastance (Ea) to ventricular elastance (Ees) is approximately 1. In heart failure, Ea is often high relative to Ees (uncoupling); vasodilators help restore this ratio, improving ejection efficiency.
Myocardial Oxygen Demand:
Wall tension is a primary determinant of myocardial oxygen consumption. By reducing afterload and systolic pressure, vasodilators significantly reduce wall tension
(Law of Laplace) and oxygen demand, which is beneficial in ischaemic heart failure.
Sodium Nitroprusside Pharmacology:
While often used in models to demonstrate afterload reduction, sodium nitroprusside is clinically a balanced vasodilator. It reduces both preload (venodilation) and
afterload (arterial dilation). In a real patient, this might reduce EDV unless fluids
are co-administered.
Law of Laplace:
Wall tension is proportional to (Pressure x Radius) / Wall Thickness. Vasodilators
reduce both pressure and the end-systolic radius, providing a dual mechanism for
reducing myocardial workload.

question: A medical student is reviewing the pharmacology of diazepam. Which of the following statements made by the student is incorrect?

options.text: 'Diazepam works by binding to the GABA-A receptor, which enhances the inhibitory effect of GABA.'
'It is highly lipophilic, which allows it to distribute widely into body tissues, including fat.'

'Because it is almost entirely metabolized in the liver, very little of the parent
drug is excreted unchanged in the urine.'

'Diazepam has a short duration of action because it is rapidly metabolised into
inactive compounds.'

'Its active metabolite, desmethyldiazepam, has a very long half-life, which can
lead to accumulation.'

correctAnswer:
'Diazepam has a short duration of action because it is rapidly metabolised into
inactive compounds.'
englishExplanation:
Analysis of the Incorrect Statement:
Option D is incorrect because diazepam is metabolised into active metabolites
(desmethyldiazepam, temazepam, and oxazepam), not inactive ones. Furthermore,
the short duration of clinical effect after a single bolus is due to redistribution to
lipid-rich tissues, not rapid metabolism. The drug itself has a long elimination halflife (20-50 hours), and the statement incorrectly attributes the short duration of action to rapid metabolism.
Metabolism and Excretion:
Diazepam undergoes hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP3A4 and CYP2C19
(Phase I demethylation and hydroxylation) to active metabolites. These are eventually conjugated with glucuronide (Phase II) and excreted in the urine. Less than 1%
of the parent drug is excreted unchanged.
Active Metabolites:
The primary metabolite, desmethyldiazepam (nordiazepam), has an elimination
half-life of 30-100+ hours. This contributes significantly to the prolonged sedative
effects and risk of accumulation, particularly in the elderly or those with hepatic
impairment.
Clinical Pearl
Active Metabolites and Accumulation:
Diazepam is characterised by a long elimination half-life and conversion to active
metabolites (desmethyldiazepam, temazepam, oxazepam), leading to significant accumulation with repeated dosing.
Mechanism of Action:
Benzodiazepines bind to the alpha-gamma subunit interface of the GABA-A receptor, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening and enhancing the inhibitory effect of GABA (allosteric modulation).
Lipophilicity and Volume of Distribution (Vd):
Highly lipophilic drugs can leave the bloodstream and enter tissues easily, resulting
in a large volume of distribution.
Clinical Use Dictated by Pharmacokinetics:
Diazepam's long half-life and active metabolites make it ideal for tapering regimens
(like in alcohol withdrawal) where a smooth, sustained effect is desired.
Hepatic Impairment Prolongs Effects:

In patients with liver disease, the metabolism of both diazepam and its metabolites
is impaired, leading to a profound and dangerously prolonged sedative effect.
Redistribution vs. Elimination:
Recovery from a single IV bolus of diazepam is due to redistribution from the central compartment to peripheral tissues (alpha phase), not metabolism. This explains
why patients wake up quickly after a single dose despite the drug's long elimination
half-life.
Propylene Glycol Toxicity:
Intravenous diazepam is formulated with propylene glycol (to improve solubility),
which can cause pain on injection, thrombophlebitis, and potential toxicity (metabolic acidosis, renal failure) with high-dose infusions.
Context-Sensitive Half-Time:
Unlike midazolam or propofol, diazepam has a context-sensitive half-time that increases rapidly and linearly with the duration of infusion, making it unsuitable for
long-term sedation in the ICU.
Solubility Comparison with Midazolam:
Diazepam is lipophilic at all pH levels and requires propylene glycol for IV formulation. Midazolam is water-soluble at pH <4 (in the ampoule) due to an open imidazole ring, which closes at physiological pH to become lipid-soluble.
Effect of Age:
In the elderly, the volume of distribution for diazepam increases (increased body
fat) and hepatic clearance decreases, significantly prolonging the elimination halflife (can exceed 100 hours).

question:
Which statement BEST distinguishes the mechanism of sirolimus from
tacrolimus?

options.text: Sirolimus inhibits calcineurin; tacrolimus inhibits mTOR
Both bind FKBP-12, but sirolimus inhibits mTOR rather than calcineurin
Sirolimus inhibits IL-2 production; tacrolimus inhibits IL-2 receptor signalling
Sirolimus depletes purine synthesis in T cells; tacrolimus blocks calcineurin

Both have identical mechanisms but different pharmacokinetic profiles

Correct answerBoth bind FKBP-12, but sirolimus inhibits mTOR rather than calcineurin

correctAnswer: Both bind FKBP-12, but sirolimus inhibits mTOR rather than calcineurin
englishExplanation:
Why This Matters:
Sirolimus and tacrolimus are frequently confused because they share the same intracellular binding protein (FKBP-12), yet have completely different downstream
targets and toxicity profiles. This distinction is a high-yield examiner favourite in
transplant pharmacology.
Analysis of Each Option:
Option A — Sirolimus inhibits calcineurin; tacrolimus inhibits mTOR:
INCORRECT — this is the exact reversal of the truth. Tacrolimus inhibits calcineurin; sirolimus inhibits mTOR. A common exam trap.
Option B — Both bind FKBP-12, sirolimus inhibits mTOR:
CORRECT. Both drugs bind FKBP-12. However: tacrolimus-FKBP-12 → inhibits
calcineurin → blocks IL-2 gene transcription (upstream of IL-2 receptor signalling).
Sirolimus-FKBP-12 → inhibits mTORC1 → blocks T-cell cycle progression from G1
to S phase (downstream of IL-2 receptor signalling, in response to IL-2 itself).
Option C — Sirolimus inhibits IL-2 production:
INCORRECT. Sirolimus does NOT block IL-2 production. It blocks the T-cell response TO IL-2 (via mTOR inhibition downstream of the IL-2 receptor). IL-2 is still
produced — it just fails to drive cell cycle progression.
Option D — Sirolimus depletes purine synthesis:
INCORRECT. Purine synthesis depletion via IMPDH inhibition is the mechanism of
mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), not sirolimus.
Option E — Identical mechanisms, different pharmacokinetics:
INCORRECT. The mechanisms are fundamentally different (calcineurin vs mTOR),
resulting in entirely different toxicity profiles and clinical indications.
Clinical Implication:
Because sirolimus acts downstream of IL-2 and tacrolimus acts upstream, they can
theoretically be used synergistically. In practice, the combination increases toxicity
without proportional immunosuppressive benefit in most transplant protocols.
Clinical Pearl
Same Binding Protein, Different Target:
Both sirolimus and tacrolimus bind FKBP-12. However the downstream targets are
completely different — tacrolimus targets calcineurin (upstream of IL-2 production)
while sirolimus targets mTORC1 (downstream of IL-2 receptor signalling).
mTOR Biology:

mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) complex 1 integrates signals from growth
factors, amino acid availability, and energy status. In T cells, IL-2 receptor activation triggers mTOR to drive cell cycle progression from G1 to S phase. Sirolimus
blocks this step.
Complementary Immunosuppression:
Because tacrolimus and sirolimus act at different points in the T-cell activation cascade (IL-2 production vs IL-2 response), they can be used synergistically. However,
combined use significantly increases nephrotoxicity risk.
No Calcineurin Nephrotoxicity:
Unlike tacrolimus and cyclosporine, sirolimus does not cause calcineurin-mediated
renal vasoconstriction. It is used in calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity as a renalsparing alternative. However, it can cause or worsen proteinuria.
Wound Healing Impairment:
Sirolimus inhibits mTOR-dependent fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis, impairing wound healing. It is typically held for several weeks before and after any
surgical procedure, including transplantation. Early post-transplant use is associated with lymphocele formation.
Dyslipidaemia:
Sirolimus commonly causes hypertriglyceridaemia and hypercholesterolaemia
(mTOR normally promotes lipid breakdown). Statin therapy is frequently required
in sirolimus-treated transplant recipients.
mTOR Pneumonitis:
Sirolimus-induced pneumonitis is a class effect of mTOR inhibitors. It presents as
non-infectious bilateral infiltrates, dry cough, and hypoxia. Diagnosis is one of exclusion; management is dose reduction or drug discontinuation. It is partially
steroid-responsive.
Antiproliferative Uses:
Sirolimus (and its analogue everolimus) exploit the anti-proliferative effects of
mTOR inhibition beyond immunosuppression — they are used as antiproliferative
coatings on drug-eluting coronary stents and as oncological agents in renal cell carcinoma and neuroendocrine tumours.
Tacrolimus Conversion:
When converting from tacrolimus to sirolimus due to nephrotoxicity, a wash-out
period is recommended, and sirolimus levels must be closely monitored as both
drugs compete for FKBP-12 binding.

question:
A 6-year-old child, who weighs 20 kg, develops acute anaphylaxis with stridor
and hypotension after a bee sting. What is the correct first-line dose and route of
administration for epinephrine (adrenaline)?

options.text: 0.5 mg of 1:1,000 solution, given intravenously (IV).
0.02 mg of 1:10,000 solution, given intravenously (IV).
0.2 mg of 1:1,000 solution, given intramuscularly (IM).
0.2 mg of 1:10,000 solution, given intramuscularly (IM).

1.0 mg of 1:10,000 solution, given intravenously (IV).

Correct answer0.2 mg of 1:1,000 solution, given intramuscularly (IM).

correctAnswer: 0.2 mg of 1:1,000 solution, given intramuscularly (IM).
englishExplanation:
First-line Treatment:
The first-line treatment for anaphylaxis is immediate intramuscular (IM) epinephrine using the 1:1,000 concentration (1 mg/mL).
Dosing Calculation (Weight vs. Age):
The gold standard weight-based dose for IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis is 10
micrograms/kg (0.01 mg/kg). For a 20 kg child: 20 kg x 0.01 mg/kg = 0.2 mg (200
micrograms). Note that RCUK guidelines also provide age-based bands for ease of
use in non-specialist settings (e.g., 300 micrograms for 6-12 years), but the precise
weight-based calculation is preferred in critical care and aligns with Option C.
Route and Concentration:
IM injection into the anterolateral thigh is the definitive first-line treatment. The
1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) concentration is used for IM administration to minimize volume. The 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) concentration is reserved for IV use. IV bolus
adrenaline is hazardous and reserved for cardiac arrest or experienced specialists
treating refractory hypotension.
Why Option B is Incorrect:
Option B (0.02 mg IV) represents a dose of 1 microgram/kg. While this is the correct magnitude for a cautious IV bolus by a specialist in refractory anaphylaxis
(titrated effect), it is NOT the first-line treatment. First-line administration is always IM.
Clinical Pearl
Concentration Safety:
Use 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) for IM administration and 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) for IV use.
Confusing these concentrations is a common cause of fatal 10-fold dosing errors.
Weight-based Dosing:
0.01 mg/kg is the key paediatric dose to remember for IM adrenaline (1:1,000).
Auto-injector Doses:
Prescribe auto-injectors by weight: 150 micrograms for 15-30 kg; 300 micrograms
for >30 kg. (Note: 300 micrograms can be considered for children 25-30 kg based
on risk).
No Contraindications:
There are no absolute contraindications to epinephrine in life-threatening
anaphylaxis.
Steroids and Antihistamines:

RCUK guidelines explicitly state NOT to use antihistamines or corticosteroids for
the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis. They do not shorten the duration of symptoms or prevent biphasic reactions and may delay adrenaline administration.
Refractory Anaphylaxis:
If there is no response to two IM adrenaline doses given 5 minutes apart, start an IV
fluid bolus (10 mL/kg) and call for expert help to consider an IV adrenaline
infusion.
Discharge Observation:
Patients with anaphylaxis require observation after symptom resolution. RCUK suggests a minimum of 6 hours for those who required 2 doses of adrenaline or had severe reactions, though local protocols vary.
Mast Cell Stabilisation:
Adrenaline works not only by reversing shock but by stopping the underlying
pathology. Beta-2 receptor activation increases cAMP, which prevents further degranulation of mast cells and histamine release.
IV Bolus Risks:
Intravenous adrenaline boluses in a patient with a palpable pulse carry a high risk
of hypertensive crisis, ventricular arrhythmias, and myocardial ischaemia. This
route is reserved for specialist use in refractory shock or cardiac arrest.
Fluid Resuscitation:
Anaphylaxis causes massive vasodilation and capillary leak (distributive shock).
Aggressive fluid resuscitation (10-20 mL/kg crystalloid) is often required alongside
adrenaline to restore preload.
Beta-Blocker Resistance:
Patients on beta-blockers may be resistant to adrenaline. Glucagon (1-5 mg IV) can
be used as an antidote; it bypasses beta-receptors to increase intracellular cAMP via
glucagon receptors.
Absorption Kinetics:
The anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis) is the preferred injection site because it has
better blood flow and faster absorption kinetics for adrenaline than the deltoid or
gluteal muscles, especially in shock states.
Biphasic Reactions:
A recurrence of symptoms after initial resolution (without re-exposure) occurs in a
small percentage of cases. This possibility necessitates the observation period posttreatment.

question:
A 55-year-old veterinarian presents with fever, myalgias, and a productive cough
after returning from a trip to the Middle East where he treated sick horses. On
examination, he has multiple painful, ulcerative skin lesions. What is the most
likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cutaneous Anthrax
Glanders
Tularemia
Brucellosis

Melioidosis

Correct answerGlanders

correctAnswer: Glanders
englishExplanation:
Pathogenesis & Epidemiology:
Glanders is a zoonotic disease caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Burkholderia
mallei. It is primarily a disease of solipeds (horses, mules, donkeys). The combination of direct contact with sick equines in an endemic region (Middle East, Asia,
South America) and a clinical syndrome of pneumonia with ulcerative skin lesions is
highly characteristic. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected secretions
or inhalation.
Differential Diagnosis:
Melioidosis, caused by the related Burkholderia pseudomallei, is clinically similar
but is acquired from environmental exposure (soil/water) rather than direct animal
contact.
Clinical Presentation:
The disease manifests as acute septicemia, pulmonary infection (pneumonia, lung
abscesses), or chronic cutaneous infection. The cutaneous form, historically known
as 'Farcy', presents with nodules along lymphatic vessels that ulcerate and discharge
pus.
Management:
Burkholderia species have intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics (including penicillin and first/second-generation cephalosporins). Treatment follows a
Melioidosis-like paradigm: an intensive IV phase (Ceftazidime or Meropenem) followed by a prolonged oral eradication phase (Co-trimoxazole).
Clinical Pearl
Zoonotic Reservoir:
The key epidemiological link is direct contact with infected solipeds (horses, donkeys, or mules).
Bioterrorism Agent:
Burkholderia mallei is a CDC Category B bioterrorism agent and is classified as a
High Consequence Infectious Disease (HCID) in the UK.
Clinical Forms:
The disease manifests as pulmonary, septicemic, or cutaneous forms. The cutaneous
form, characterized by lymphatic thickening and ulcerative nodules, is historically
termed 'Farcy'.
Geographic Distribution:

Glanders has been eradicated in North America and Western Europe but remains
endemic in parts of the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and South America.
Differentiation from Melioidosis:
Glanders is acquired via direct animal contact, whereas Melioidosis is acquired via
environmental (soil/water) exposure.
Microbiological Distinction:
Burkholderia mallei is non-motile, whereas the closely related Burkholderia pseudomallei (Melioidosis) is motile.
Antibiotic Resistance Profile:
Burkholderia species are intrinsically resistant to penicillins, ampicillin,
first/second-generation cephalosporins, gentamicin, and tobramycin. Ceftazidime
or Carbapenems are the agents of choice.
Laboratory Safety:
Due to high aerosol infectivity, laboratory samples suspected of containing B. mallei
must be handled in a Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) facility.
Pain Characteristics:
A key discriminator between cutaneous Glanders and Anthrax is pain; Glanders lesions are typically painful, whereas the eschar of cutaneous Anthrax is characteristically painless.
Eradication Therapy:
Similar to Melioidosis, preventing relapse requires a prolonged eradication phase
(minimum 12 weeks) with oral co-trimoxazole or doxycycline after the initial intensive intravenous phase.
Radiological Features:
Pulmonary Glanders typically presents with lobar pneumonia, bronchopneumonia,
or lung abscesses. Cavitation is common and may mimic tuberculosis or
melioidosis.

question:
A patient with a massive pulmonary embolism is started on an unfractionated
heparin infusion. Despite escalating the dose to a very high rate (e.g., 40
units/kg/hr), the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) remains subtherapeutic. This "heparin resistance" is most commonly caused by a deficiency of
which protein?

options.text: Factor VIII
Protein C
Antithrombin III
Fibrinogen

Plasminogen

Correct answerAntithrombin III

correctAnswer: Antithrombin III
englishExplanation:
Mechanism of Action:
Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is an indirect anticoagulant. It binds to
Antithrombin (AT), inducing a conformational change that accelerates AT's inhibition of Thrombin (Factor IIa) and Factor Xa by 1,000-fold. Without adequate AT,
heparin is ineffective regardless of the dose.
Defining Heparin Resistance:
Heparin resistance is clinically defined as the requirement for >35,000 units of
UFH per 24 hours to prolong the aPTT into the therapeutic range. It can also be defined as an inability to achieve a therapeutic aPTT despite escalating doses.
True vs. Pseudo-Resistance:
Resistance can be 'True' (low AT levels, increased heparin clearance, or increased
heparin-binding proteins) or 'Pseudo' (dissociation between aPTT and heparin levels). Pseudo-resistance is common in critical illness where acute phase reactants
like Factor VIII and Fibrinogen are elevated. These proteins shorten the aPTT, making it appear subtherapeutic even when heparin levels (measured by Anti-Xa) are
adequate.
Management:
1. Verify resistance by checking an Anti-Xa level. If Anti-Xa is therapeutic but aPTT
is low, do not increase the dose (Pseudo-resistance).
2. If both are low (True resistance), consider switching to a direct thrombin inhibitor (Argatroban, Bivalirudin) or, less commonly, supplementing Antithrombin.
Clinical Pearl
No Antithrombin, No Heparin Effect:
This is the key concept. Heparin is just a catalyst for the body's own Antithrombin.
Measure an Anti-Xa Level:
The Anti-Xa assay is the gold standard for distinguishing true from pseudo-resistance. If aPTT is subtherapeutic but Anti-Xa is therapeutic (0.3-0.7 IU/mL), the patient is anticoagulated; do not increase the dose. This is 'pseudo-resistance' caused
by high Factor VIII.
Treatment:
While FFP or AT concentrates can restore efficacy, they are costly or volume-heavy.
The preferred management for true heparin resistance in the UK is switching to a
Direct Thrombin Inhibitor (DTI) like Argatroban or Bivalirudin, which act independently of Antithrombin.

LMWH vs. UFH Potency:
Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) has a higher Anti-Xa to Anti-IIa ratio
(ranging from 2:1 to 4:1) compared to UFH (1:1). While LMWH relies less on thrombin inhibition, it still requires Antithrombin for its action and will also be ineffective
in severe Antithrombin deficiency.
Causes of Acquired AT Deficiency:
Critical illness frequently depletes Antithrombin. Key causes include sepsis (consumption), DIC, liver failure (reduced synthesis), nephrotic syndrome (urinary
loss), and bypass circuits (ECMO/CPB).
The Factor VIII Confounder:
Factor VIII is an acute phase reactant. High levels (common in
inflammation/infection) shorten the aPTT in vitro. This masks the anticoagulant effect of heparin on the aPTT test, leading to potentially dangerous dose escalations if
Anti-Xa monitoring is not used.
Heparin Resistance Threshold:
Suspect resistance if the patient requires >35,000 units/24 hours or escalating boluses fail to move the aPTT. Early recognition prevents thrombotic progression.
Argatroban and INR Monitoring:
Argatroban is a common alternative in heparin resistance (and HIT), but it falsely
elevates the INR. When bridging to warfarin, the target INR is often set higher (e.g.,
greater than 4.0) before stopping the infusion to ensure therapeutic oral
anticoagulation.
DTI Clearance Mechanisms:
Choice of alternative anticoagulant depends on organ function. Argatroban is hepatically cleared and contraindicated in severe liver failure (Child-Pugh C). Bivalirudin
is cleared by a combination of proteolytic degradation (20%) and renal mechanisms
(80% of the remainder), requiring dose adjustment in renal failure.
Spectrum of Inhibition:
The Heparin-Antithrombin complex inhibits not only Thrombin (IIa) and Xa, but
also factors IXa, XIa, and XIIa. This broad activity explains why UFH is monitored
via the intrinsic pathway (aPTT).
Antithrombin Physiology:
Antithrombin is a serine protease inhibitor synthesized in the liver with a half-life of
approximately 3 days. Normal plasma activity is 80-120%. Heparin resistance is
typically seen when levels fall below 60%.

question:
A 63-year-old patient with a massive PE is in shock with RV strain on echo. He
has a history of an ischemic stroke 2 months ago. What is the most appropriate
management?

options.text: Immediate systemic thrombolysis with alteplase.
Immediate anticoagulation with heparin and consideration of surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy.
Placement of an IVC filter and fluid resuscitation.
Start an oral anticoagulant like rivaroxaban.
High-dose intravenous corticosteroids.

correctAnswer: Immediate anticoagulation with heparin and consideration of surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy.
englishExplanation:
Introduction:
This patient has a massive PE but also has a major, absolute contraindication to systemic thrombolysis.
Contraindications to Thrombolysis:
A history of ischaemic stroke within the preceding 6 months is an absolute contraindication to systemic thrombolysis according to ESC guidelines (widely
adopted in UK practice). The risk of haemorrhagic transformation is prohibitively
high. Other absolute contraindications include active bleeding, recent major surgery
or trauma, and any history of haemorrhagic stroke or CNS neoplasm.
Management Rationale:
Since systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated, mechanical reperfusion is required.
Immediate anticoagulation with Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) is the crucial
first step to prevent clot propagation. Definitive options include:
•Surgical Embolectomy: The preferred option in many centres for patients with
absolute contraindications to lysis, provided surgical expertise is available.
•Catheter-Directed Treatment: Percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy or
fragmentation is an alternative. Note that catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT)
may still be risky given the recent stroke, making mechanical techniques preferable.
Conclusion:
The correct pathway is to start heparin and then urgently consult interventional
radiology/cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery to decide on the best reperfusion
strategy.
Clinical Pearl
Check Contraindications:
Always verify absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis. For PE, ischaemic stroke
within the preceding 6 months is an absolute contraindication (ESC guidelines), differing from the 3-month window often cited for acute ischaemic stroke lysis
eligibility.
Heparin is Still Important:
Initiate Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) immediately in high-risk PE. Its short halflife and reversibility with protamine make it the anticoagulant of choice when imminent surgical or catheter intervention is possible.
Surgical vs. Catheter-Based:

The choice between surgical embolectomy and catheter-directed therapy depends
on patient stability, clot location, available expertise, and institutional resources.
IVC Filters:
An IVC filter (C) does not treat the current PE. It is used to prevent future PEs in
patients who have a contraindication to anticoagulation.
ECMO as a Bridge:
In a patient with massive PE and profound circulatory collapse, veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) can be used as a bridge to stabilize
the patient while definitive clot removal is arranged.
Definition of Massive PE:
Massive PE (High-risk PE) is defined by haemodynamic instability (cardiac arrest,
obstructive shock, or persistent hypotension <90 mmHg), not by the anatomical
burden of the clot on CT.
Mechanism of Heparin:
Unfractionated heparin acts by binding to Antithrombin III, accelerating its inhibition of Thrombin (IIa) and Factor Xa by approximately 1000-fold. It prevents
thrombus extension but relies on the endogenous fibrinolytic system to dissolve the
clot.
Fluid Management Caution:
Use fluids cautiously in massive PE. While preload is needed, excessive fluid causes
RV over-distension, worsening septal bowing into the LV and further compromising
cardiac output via interventricular dependence.
Vasopressor Choice:
Noradrenaline is preferred to maintain systemic blood pressure and RV coronary
perfusion pressure. Pure inotropes (e.g., dobutamine) can cause vasodilation and
hypotension if used without vasopressor support.
Catheter-Directed Therapies:
Options include mechanical fragmentation, aspiration thrombectomy, or rheolytic
thrombectomy. These avoid systemic thrombolytic exposure, making them suitable
for patients with high bleeding risk.
VA-ECMO Configuration:
In massive PE, Veno-Arterial (VA) ECMO is required to bypass the pulmonary circulation and provide haemodynamic support. Veno-Venous (VV) ECMO is insufficient as it does not unload the RV.
